Hydraulic Fluids Used for Lubrication of System Components Hydraulic fluid lubricates pump pistons, valve spools, cylinder rods, and motor bearings by forming a hydrodynamic film of 1 to 10 micrometers between moving surfaces at relative velocities from 1 to 10 meters per second. Anti-wear additives containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDDP) at concentrations from 0.05% to 0.15% protect surfaces operating under boundary lubrication conditions at contact pressures from 50,000 psi to 200,000 psi at the asperity level inside axial piston pumps. Maintaining fluid viscosity above the minimum specification of 10 centistokes at maximum operating temperature preserves the lubricating film and prevents pump service life reduction from 10,000 hours to below 2,000 hours caused by metal-to-metal contact under collapsed film conditions. "As design engineers, we often focus so much on sizing heavy steel cylinders and selecting powerful pumps that we treat hydraulic fluid as an afterthought (just something you buy by the bucket to fill the circuit). But the reality is that fluid functions as a critical moving component within our assembly, squeezing through precision clearances as small as a human blood cell. If we do not explicitly design around how that fluid thins out under heat or chemically attacks our seals, even the most robust mechanical design on paper will fail catastrophically in the field." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering 8. Hydraulic Fluids Used for Heat Transfer and Cooling Hydraulic fluid removes heat generated by pressure drops across valves, internal pump and motor leakage, and mechanical friction by carrying thermal energy from the circuit back to the reservoir and heat exchanger for dissipation. A standard industrial hydraulic system generates heat at 20% to 30% of total input power, meaning a 50-horsepower system produces 10 to 15 horsepower of heat that the fluid must transport continuously to the cooling circuit. Fluid specific heat capacity from 1.67 to 2.09 kJ per kilogram per degree Celsius for mineral oils determines the volume of fluid required to absorb the heat load without exceeding the maximum operating temperature of 80°C to 90°C for petroleum-based grades in continuous duty operation. What Are the Advantages of Using Hydraulic Fluid? The advantages of using hydraulic fluid are listed below. High Power Density : Hydraulic fluid transmits forces from 1,000 pounds to over 5,000 tons through compact hoses and cylinders at pressures from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi, achieving power density no pneumatic or mechanical system matches at equivalent component size. Simultaneous Lubrication : The same fluid that transmits power lubricates every internal moving surface it contacts, eliminating the need for separate lubrication systems in pumps, valves, and actuators. Effective Heat Dissipation: Hydraulic fluid carries thermal energy from pressure drops and pump friction to the reservoir and heat exchanger, maintaining system temperature below 60°C to 65°C across continuous duty cycles. Precise Controllability : Proportional flow control valves modulate fluid delivery to actuators continuously from 0 to maximum speed without discrete steps, enabling exact force and position control over loads from 50 pounds to thousands of tons. Overload Protection : Pressure relief valves preset from 500 psi to 5,000 psi divert excess fluid to the reservoir automatically when system load exceeds design limits, protecting all downstream components without operator intervention. Versatility Across Fluid Types : Petroleum-based, synthetic, biodegradable, water-based, and fire-resistant hydraulic fluid formulations cover operating environments from arctic construction sites to aircraft engine bays, making the hydraulic power transmission concept adaptable to nearly every industrial and mobile application. events.after: Resources / Machining Design / 5 Types of Hydraulic Fluid 5 Types of Hydraulic Fluid Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 25 min read Published June 22, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Hydraulic fluid is a liquid medium that transmits power, lubricates internal components, and dissipates heat within a hydraulic system. The hydraulic fluid fills the entire circuit from reservoir to actuator, carrying pressure energy generated by the pump to cylinders and motors performing mechanical work. Selecting the correct fluid type determines system efficiency, component lifespan, and operational safety across every application. Hydraulic fluid is important because it governs pressure transmission, surface lubrication, and thermal regulation simultaneously. A system running degraded or incompatible fluid loses volumetric efficiency, accelerates seal and pump wear, and risks catastrophic component failure. Operating pressures from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi demand a fluid with adequate viscosity, thermal stability, and chemical compatibility with seals and metals throughout the circuit. Different hydraulic fluid types interact with system components in distinct ways. Mineral-based fluids provide reliable lubrication in standard industrial equipment, water-based fluids offer fire resistance in high-heat environments, synthetic fluids maintain stability at temperature extremes, biodegradable fluids reduce environmental risk in sensitive areas, and fire-resistant fluids protect personnel and equipment in steel plants and aviation facilities. Matching the fluid type to the operating environment determines whether the hydraulic system performs reliably across its full service life. 1. Mineral Based (Petroleum) Hydraulic Fluids Mineral-based hydraulic fluid is refined from crude oil and represents the most widely used hydraulic fluid type across industrial, construction, and mobile equipment applications. The fluid delivers reliable lubrication at viscosity grades from ISO VG 32 to ISO VG 68 and performs at operating temperatures from 0°C to 90°C. Petroleum-based fluids cost [$2 to $8] per liter, making them the most affordable option in the hydraulic fluid category. Pros : Affordable and widely available, with strong lubrication performance and broad compatibility with standard seals, hoses, and pump materials. Cons : Flammable with flash points from 150°C to 220°C, and a petroleum-based composition presents environmental contamination risk in the event of leakage. 2. Water Based Hydraulic Fluids Water-based hydraulic fluids incorporate water as the primary fire-suppression component and appear in three distinct subtypes serving different performance requirements. Water-Glycol Fluids mix water and glycol in ratios from 35% to 50% water content, achieving fire resistance without a measurable flash point while maintaining viscosity suitable for system pressures up to 2,500 psi. Oil-in-Water Emulsions suspend small oil droplets in a water carrier, providing moderate lubrication with water content from 85% to 95% and fire resistance at temperatures above 5 to 50 °C. Water-in-Oil Emulsions disperse water droplets within an oil continuous phase, delivering better lubrication than oil-in-water types with water content from 40% to 45%. Pros : Fire-resistant and effective at cooling system components during high-heat operation. Cons : Lower lubrication capacity than mineral oil, with corrosion risk to ferrous metals if the concentration and pH from 8.5 to 9.5 are not maintained. 3. Synthetic Hydraulic Fluids Synthetic hydraulic fluids are engineered from chemical compounds rather than refined crude oil, designed to perform where mineral-based fluids fail due to temperature extremes or fire risk. Phosphate esters, silicones, and polyalphaolefins (PAO) represent the primary synthetic types, with operating temperature ranges from -54°C to 135°C for PAO grades and up to 250°C for silicone-based fluids. Synthetic fluids cost [$15 to $60] per liter, depending on base chemistry and additive package. Pros : Excellent thermal and oxidative stability, high-temperature resistance, and fire-resistant properties in phosphate ester grades used in aviation and steel industries. Cons : High cost relative to mineral and water-based alternatives, with potential incompatibility with standard nitrile seals requiring fluorocarbon or EPDM seal substitution. 4. Biodegradable (Environmentally Friendly) Fluids Biodegradable hydraulic fluids derive from vegetable oils (rapeseed, sunflower, or soybean) or synthetic esters designed to minimize ecological impact in the event of leakage or spill. The fluids biodegrade at rates from 70% to 99% within 28 days under OECD 301B testing standards, compared to less than 30% biodegradability for mineral-based alternatives. Cost ranges from [$8 to $25] per liter depending on base oil type and additive content. Pros : Environmentally safe, low toxicity, and preferred for forestry, marine, and agricultural equipment operating near water sources or ecologically sensitive areas. Cons : Shorter service life from 2,000 to 4,000 hours compared to 4,000 to 8,000 hours for mineral oil, and higher susceptibility to oxidative degradation at temperatures above 70°C. 5. Fire Resistant Hydraulic Fluids Fire-resistant hydraulic fluids serve applications where ignition risk from hot surfaces, open flames, or molten metal contact is a primary operational hazard. Steel plants, die casting facilities, mining equipment, and aviation hydraulic systems specify fire-resistant fluids to protect personnel and equipment from fluid ignition in environments where hot surface exposure exceeds 300°C. The category includes water-based fluids (water-glycol and emulsions) and synthetic fluids (phosphate esters and polyol esters), with prices ranging from [$10 to $50] per liter. Pros : Significantly safer in high-heat and ignition-risk environments, with phosphate ester fluids achieving self-extinguishing behavior under direct flame exposure. Cons : Higher cost than mineral-based alternatives, with synthetic fire-resistant fluids requiring system compatibility verification for seals, paints, and non-ferrous metals before installation. What Is Hydraulic Fluid? Hydraulic fluid is an incompressible liquid that transmits power through a sealed hydraulic circuit by carrying pressure energy from the pump to actuators performing mechanical work. The fluid fills every component continuously, from the reservoir through the pump, valve block, hoses, and cylinder, maintaining a pressure pathway that converts pump output into usable force at the actuator. Beyond power transmission, hydraulic fluid lubricates all internal moving surfaces, including pump pistons, valve spools, and cylinder rods, forming a hydrodynamic film of 1 to 10 micrometers that prevents metal-to-metal contact at operating velocities. The fluid transfers heat generated by pressure drops and internal friction back to the reservoir and heat exchanger, maintaining system temperature within the acceptable range of 40°C to 80°C for most industrial applications. Fluid properties, including viscosity, bulk modulus, flash point, and additive chemistry, determine compatibility with system components and suitability for the operating environment. Petroleum-based, water-based, synthetic, biodegradable, and fire-resistant formulations each represent a category of Hydraulic Fluid serving distinct pressure, temperature, and environmental requirements. How Does a Hydraulic System Work with Different Hydraulic Fluid Types? A hydraulic system works by the same fundamental pressure transmission principle regardless of fluid type, but the fluid's viscosity, compressibility, and lubrication capacity directly affect how efficiently the system converts pump output into actuator force. Pascal's Law governs pressure transmission in every fluid type, confirming that pressure applied at the pump transmits equally throughout the circuit to the actuator. Mineral-based fluids at ISO VG 46 maintain viscosity near 46 centistokes at 40°C, providing reliable film thickness across standard industrial pump clearances of 0.0002 inch to 0.0006 inch. Water-based fluids with lower viscosity from 15 to 35 centistokes reduce lubrication film thickness, increasing internal leakage and lowering volumetric efficiency by 3% to 8% compared to mineral oil in the same pump. Synthetic fluids maintain stable viscosity across temperature ranges from -54°C to 135°C, allowing consistent system performance where mineral oil would thicken at cold start or thin excessively at high operating temperature. The relationship from fluid type to How does a Hydraulic System Work confirms that viscosity grade selection determines pump efficiency, actuator speed consistency, and component wear rate across every operating condition. Does Fluid Type Affect How a Hydraulic System Works? Yes, fluid type affects how a hydraulic system works by influencing viscosity, lubrication film thickness, volumetric efficiency, and thermal behavior throughout the operating cycle. The pressure transmission principle remains constant across all fluid types, but efficiency and component durability change significantly depending on fluid selection. A system designed for ISO VG 46 mineral oil operating on water-glycol fluid at 30 centistokes experiences increased internal leakage across pump and valve clearances, reducing volumetric efficiency and lowering actuator force output at the same pump speed. Water-based fluids also require system pressure de-rating by 10% to 20% compared to mineral oil specifications to prevent accelerated wear on pump and motor components rated for oil lubrication. Synthetic fluids in the same system maintain stable viscosity across a wider temperature range, improving cold-start performance and reducing thermal degradation at sustained high loads. Matching fluid type to system design specifications determines whether the hydraulic circuit meets its rated pressure, flow, and service life targets in actual operation. Why Is Hydraulic Fluid Important in Hydraulic Systems? Hydraulic fluid is important in hydraulic systems because it performs power transmission, lubrication, heat removal, and contamination control simultaneously within a single fluid body. Removing or degrading any one of the functions collapses system performance and accelerates component failure across the entire circuit. Power transmission depends on the fluid's incompressibility, with a bulk modulus from 200,000 psi to 300,000 psi for petroleum-based oils, ensuring immediate pressure response at the actuator. Lubrication depends on maintaining adequate viscosity at operating temperature, with film thickness below 1 micrometer causing boundary lubrication conditions that increase pump wear rates by a factor of 3 to 10. Heat removal capacity determines whether the fluid carries thermal energy from valve pressure drops and pump friction to the reservoir and heat exchanger without exceeding the maximum fluid temperature of 80°C to 90°C for mineral-based grades. Contaminated or degraded fluid causes 70% to 80% of all hydraulic system failures, confirming that fluid condition in Hydraulic Systems governs reliability more than component design or operating pressure alone. What Happens If the Wrong Hydraulic Oil Is Used in a Hydraulic System? The reasons if wrong hydraulic oil is used in a hydraulic system are listed below. Accelerated Pump Wear : An incompatible fluid with viscosity below the pump's minimum specification reduces hydrodynamic film thickness below 1 micrometer, causing boundary lubrication and metal-to-metal contact that shortens pump service life from 10,000 hours to below 2,000 hours. Seal Degradation : Fluids chemically incompatible with system seal materials cause swelling, shrinkage, or hardening of nitrile, polyurethane, or EPDM seals within 500 to 2,000 operating hours, resulting in internal and external leakage at pressures from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi. Reduced Volumetric Efficiency: A fluid with viscosity too low for system clearances of 0.0002 inch to 0.0006 inch increases internal leakage across pump and motor components, dropping volumetric efficiency below 85% and reducing actuator force and speed at the same pump output. Overheating : Fluids with inadequate thermal stability or viscosity index oxidize at temperatures above 80°C, forming sludge and varnish deposits on valve spools and pump internals that restrict flow and trap heat within the circuit. Corrosion of Metal Components : Water-based fluids applied outside their specified pH range from 8.5 to 9.5 corrode ferrous and non-ferrous metal surfaces, producing particulate contamination that circulates through the circuit and damages precision components. Can the Wrong Fluid Damage a Hydraulic System? Yes, the wrong fluid damages a hydraulic system, and the damage progresses rapidly once an incompatible fluid enters the circuit. Seal materials, pump internals, valve spools, and metal surfaces all respond to fluid chemistry and viscosity within hours to days of exposure, depending on operating pressure and temperature. A phosphate ester synthetic fluid introduced into a system with standard nitrile seals dissolves seal material within 24 to 48 hours causing seal failure and uncontrolled leakage at every static and dynamic sealing point in the circuit. A mineral oil with viscosity grade ISO VG 100 installed in a system specified for ISO VG 32 increases flow resistance across valve passages and reduces pump delivery at cold start temperatures below 20°C, causing cavitation-induced damage to pump inlet components within the first operating hours. Flushing the system with the correct fluid after contamination removes residual incompatible fluid, but components already damaged by wear, corrosion, or seal degradation require inspection and replacement before reliable operation resumes. How Do Hydraulic Fluid Properties Impact System Performance? Hydraulic fluid properties impact system performance by determining how efficiently pressure transmits from the pump to the actuator, how effectively internal surfaces are lubricated, and how well the fluid resists degradation across the operating temperature and pressure range. Each property influences a different aspect of system behavior, and no single property operates independently of the others. Viscosity governs internal leakage, pressure drop across valve passages, and hydrodynamic film thickness at pump and motor surfaces. Bulk modulus determines pressure response speed, with higher values producing faster actuator response to control inputs. Flash point and fire resistance determine safe operating environments, with mineral oils limited to non-ignition-risk areas and synthetic or water-based fluids required where open flames or molten metal are present. Oxidative stability, measured by the rotating pressure vessel oxidation test (RPVOT), determines fluid service life from 1,000 hours for vegetable-based fluids to over 8,000 hours for premium synthetic grades. Additive packages including anti-wear, anti-foam, rust inhibitors, and demulsifiers extend individual property performance across the service interval without altering the base fluid chemistry. How Does Viscosity Influence How a Hydraulic System Works? Viscosity influences how a hydraulic system works by controlling internal leakage across pump and valve clearances, pressure drop through circuit passages, and hydrodynamic film thickness at all lubricated surfaces simultaneously. The relationship from viscosity to system performance is direct and measurable at every operating temperature. A fluid with viscosity too low for the pump's internal clearances of 0.0002 inch to 0.0006 inch allows excessive leakage across piston shoes, valve plates, and spool lands, reducing volumetric efficiency below 90% and wasting pump output as heat. A fluid with viscosity too high increases pressure drop across valve orifices and pump inlet passages, raising the minimum starting temperature required for reliable operation and causing cavitation damage at the pump inlet below 0°C for high-viscosity grades. ISO VG 46 at 40°C maintains a kinematic viscosity of approximately 46 centistokes, providing the balance of leakage control and flow resistance required for most industrial hydraulic circuits operating at pressures from 1,500 psi to 3,500 psi and temperatures from 40°C to 80°C. The viscosity index (VI) measures viscosity stability across temperature, with higher VI values from 95 to 150 indicating less viscosity change from cold to hot operating conditions. Does Fluid Thickness Change Hydraulic Efficiency? Yes, fluid thickness (viscosity) changes hydraulic efficiency in two opposing ways depending on whether viscosity is above or below the system's optimum range. Volumetric efficiency and mechanical efficiency respond in opposite directions to viscosity changes, creating a performance optimum at the specified viscosity grade for each system design. Volumetric efficiency increases with higher viscosity because a thicker fluid reduces internal leakage across pump and motor clearances, keeping more pump output available as useful flow to the actuator. Mechanical efficiency decreases with higher viscosity because a thicker fluid generates greater resistance to flow through valve passages and hose circuits, requiring more pump input power to overcome internal friction losses. Below the optimum viscosity, volumetric efficiency drops due to leakage, while mechanical efficiency improves due to lower flow resistance. Overall hydraulic system efficiency, combining volumetric and mechanical factors, peaks at the viscosity grade where leakage losses and flow resistance losses are balanced. For most axial piston pumps, peak overall efficiency occurs at viscosities from 25 to 36 centistokes at operating temperature. How Do Hydraulic Systems Perform Under Different Fluid Grades? Hydraulic systems perform differently under each fluid grade because viscosity grade determines internal leakage magnitude, pump volumetric efficiency, actuator speed at a given flow rate, and component wear rate across the operating temperature range. A system tested at ISO VG 32 and ISO VG 68 in the same circuit under identical conditions produces measurably different efficiency, temperature, and wear results. ISO VG 32 reduces flow resistance in cold conditions and suits high-speed, low-pressure circuits at 1,000 psi to 2,000 psi where low starting viscosity is required. ISO VG 46 delivers the best overall efficiency balance for most industrial circuits at 1,500 psi to 3,500 psi operating at 40°C to 80°C. ISO VG 68 provides greater film thickness for heavily loaded, slow-speed circuits at pressures from 3,000 psi to 5,000 psi, where leakage control and wear protection outweigh flow resistance concerns. Mismatching the fluid grade to system design shifts the efficiency optimum outside the normal operating range, increasing heat generation by 5% to 15% and reducing component service life proportionally at sustained full-load operation. How Do ISO Hydraulic Oil Grades Affect Hydraulic System Operation? ISO hydraulic oil grades affect system operation by establishing the viscosity level at which the pump, valves, and actuators operate, with each grade number representing the fluid's kinematic viscosity in centistokes measured at 40°C. ISO VG 32, VG 46, and VG 68 represent the three most common industrial hydraulic grades, and each produces distinct pump efficiency, actuator speed, and heat generation characteristics in the same system. ISO VG 32 at 40°C maintains approximately 32 centistokes, making it suitable for high-speed vane pump circuits and cold-climate mobile equipment where low-temperature starting viscosity must remain below 1,000 centistokes. ISO VG 46 at 40°C maintains approximately 46 centistokes, covering the widest range of industrial applications, including injection molding machines, hydraulic presses, and material handling equipment at ambient temperatures from 15°C to 40°C. ISO VG 68 at 40°C maintains approximately 68 centistokes, providing greater film thickness protection for heavily loaded gear pump circuits and large cylinders operating at slow speeds and high pressures from 3,000 psi to 5,000 psi. Changing ISO grade without adjusting system relief valve settings, cooler capacity, or filter ratings produces measurable changes in operating temperature and actuator response speed. Does Oil Grade Impact Pressure and Flow in a Hydraulic System? Yes, oil grade impacts pressure and flow in a hydraulic system by altering internal leakage magnitude and flow resistance throughout the circuit. Pressure and flow are not independent of fluid viscosity, and a grade change affects both parameters simultaneously. A higher viscosity grade (ISO VG 68 replacing ISO VG 46) increases pressure drop across valve orifices, filter elements, and hose circuits because thicker fluid generates greater resistance to flow at the same flow rate. The pump must generate a higher inlet vacuum to draw the thicker fluid from the reservoir, increasing cavitation risk at ambient temperatures below 15°C. Relief valve cracking pressure appears to rise because higher flow resistance elevates system pressure at the same pump output, reducing net flow delivered to the actuator. A lower viscosity grade (ISO VG 32 replacing ISO VG 46) reduces flow resistance and pressure drop through the circuit but increases internal leakage across pump clearances by 5% to 15%, lowering effective flow to the actuator and reducing cylinder speed at the same system pressure setting. How Do You Choose the Right Hydraulic Fluid? Choosing the right hydraulic fluid requires matching the fluid's viscosity grade, base chemistry, and additive package to the system's operating pressure, temperature range, component materials, and environmental conditions. No single fluid suits every application, and selecting by cost alone without considering compatibility and performance requirements leads to premature component failure. The equipment manufacturer's specification provides the primary selection criteria, listing the required ISO viscosity grade, approved base fluid type, and minimum additive standards (anti-wear, rust inhibition, and demulsibility). Systems operating at pressures above 3,000 psi and temperatures from 60°C to 90°C require fluids with a viscosity index above 140 and oxidative stability exceeding 300 minutes by RPVOT testing. Applications near water sources or in ecologically sensitive areas require biodegradable fluids meeting OECD 301B standards with biodegradability above 60%. Fire-risk environments, including steel plants and die casting facilities, require fire-resistant fluids with flash points above 250°C or self-extinguishing behavior for phosphate ester grades. Fluid compatibility with seal materials (nitrile, polyurethane, Viton, or EPDM) must be confirmed before commissioning any new fluid type in an existing system. What Type of Hydraulic Oil Should You Use for Your Equipment? The hydraulic oil type for specific equipment depends on the manufacturer's viscosity specification, the operating temperature range, the system's maximum pressure, and the environmental conditions surrounding the equipment. Each equipment category carries distinct requirements that determine which fluid type performs reliably across the full service interval. Industrial hydraulic machinery (presses, injection molding machines, and material handling equipment) operating at 40°C to 80°C and 1,500 psi to 4,500 psi performs reliably on ISO VG 46 anti-wear mineral hydraulic oil meeting DIN 51524 Part 2 (HLP) specifications. Mobile construction equipment operating in ambient temperatures from -20°C to 40°C requires a wide viscosity index fluid at ISO VG 46 or a multigrade hydraulic oil (15W-40 or 10W-40) to maintain adequate viscosity at cold start without excessive thinning at peak operating temperature. Forestry, agricultural, and marine equipment operating near water or ecologically protected areas requires biodegradable hydraulic fluid meeting VDMA 24568 or ISO 15380 Type HETG or HEES standards. Aviation and steel plant hydraulic systems specify phosphate ester or polyol ester fire-resistant fluids meeting OEM requirements from manufacturers, including Skydrol, Fyrquel, or equivalent approved grades. Can You Use Hydraulic Oil Instead of Hydraulic Fluid? Yes, hydraulic oil functions as hydraulic fluid in most industrial and mobile hydraulic systems, and the two terms are frequently used interchangeably in maintenance and technical documentation. Hydraulic oil is a subset of hydraulic fluid, referring specifically to petroleum-based or synthetic oil formulations, while hydraulic fluid is the broader category that includes water-based and biodegradable types. A system specified for hydraulic oil operates correctly on mineral-based ISO VG 46 hydraulic oil, which meets the viscosity, lubrication, and chemical compatibility requirements for standard pumps, valves, and seals. The substitution becomes problematic when a system designed for fire-resistant hydraulic fluid (water-glycol or phosphate ester) receives petroleum-based hydraulic oil instead, because the oil lacks the fire-resistant properties the application requires and may create ignition risk in high-heat environments. Confirming that the selected hydraulic oil meets the equipment manufacturer's viscosity grade, additive standard, and material compatibility requirements before filling the system prevents the component damage and efficiency losses that fluid misapplication causes in operation. What Are the Uses of Hydraulic Fluid? The uses of hydraulic fluid are listed below. Power Transmission in Machinery : Hydraulic fluid transmits pump-generated pressure to actuators performing mechanical work in presses, injection molding machines, and material handling equipment at pressures from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi. Automotive Hydraulic Systems : Hydraulic fluid in brake systems transmits pedal force to caliper pistons at line pressures from 300 psi to 1,500 psi, while power steering fluid operates rack and pinion systems at 800 psi to 1,500 psi. Industrial Equipment Operation : Hydraulic fluid powers cylinders and motors in CNC machines, stamping presses, and industrial robots requiring precise force and speed control across variable load conditions. Aviation Systems : Phosphate ester fire-resistant hydraulic fluid at 3,000 psi to 5,000 psi actuates flight control surfaces, landing gear, and thrust reversers in commercial and military aircraft. Marine Applications : Hydraulic fluid powers steering systems, deck cranes, and stabilizer fins on commercial vessels, with biodegradable fluids specified in environmentally protected waters. Construction Machinery : Hydraulic fluid at 3,500 psi to 5,000 psi powers boom, arm, bucket, and travel systems on excavators, cranes, and bulldozers. Lubrication of System Components : Hydraulic fluid forms hydrodynamic lubricating films of 1 to 10 micrometers on pump pistons, valve spools, and cylinder rods, preventing metal-to-metal contact at operating velocities. Heat Transfer and Cooling : Hydraulic fluid carries thermal energy from pressure drops and pump friction back to the reservoir and heat exchanger, maintaining system temperature below 80°C to 90°C for mineral-based grades. 1. Hydraulic Fluids Used for Power Transmission in Machinery Hydraulic fluid transmits mechanical power from the pump to actuators by carrying pressure energy through the circuit at operating levels from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi in standard industrial machinery. The fluid's incompressibility, with a bulk modulus from 200,000 psi to 300,000 psi, ensures that pressure generated at the pump reaches the cylinder or motor without significant energy absorption in transit. ISO VG 46 mineral hydraulic oil serves as the standard power transmission fluid in presses, injection molding machines, and automated manufacturing equipment operating at temperatures from 40°C to 80°C and continuous duty cycles exceeding 8,000 hours per service interval. 2. Hydraulic Fluids Used in Automotive Hydraulic Systems Hydraulic fluid in automotive braking systems transmits pedal force through DOT 3, DOT 4, or DOT 5.1 glycol-ether or silicone brake fluid to caliper pistons at line pressures from 300 psi to 1,500 psi. Power steering systems use dedicated power steering fluid or compatible ATF (automatic transmission fluid) at operating pressures from 800 psi to 1,500 psi to actuate rack and pinion or recirculating ball steering gears. Automotive hydraulic clutch systems use DOT 3 or DOT 4 fluid at pressures from 100 psi to 600 psi to disengage the clutch plate through a slave cylinder mounted at the transmission. 3. Hydraulic Fluids Used in Industrial Equipment Operation Industrial hydraulic equipment, including CNC machining centers, hydraulic bending brakes, die casting machines, and robotic assembly systems, specifies anti-wear hydraulic oil meeting DIN 51524 Part 2 (HLP) or ISO 11158 Type HM standards at viscosity grades from ISO VG 32 to ISO VG 68. The fluid provides continuous lubrication for servo valve spools operating at clearances below 0.00004 to 0.00015 inch and piston pump components cycling at pressures from 2,000 psi to 4,500 psi across production shifts lasting 16 to 24 hours. Fluid change intervals in industrial equipment range from 2,000 hours to 8,000 hours, depending on system cleanliness level (ISO 4406 cleanliness target 16/14/11 to 17/15/12) and operating temperature history. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo 4. Hydraulic Fluids Used in Aviation Systems Aviation hydraulic systems specify phosphate ester fire-resistant fluid (Skydrol 500B-4, Skydrol LD-4, or equivalent) operating at 3,000 psi to 5,000 psi to actuate flight control surfaces, landing gear, thrust reversers, and wheel brakes on commercial and military aircraft. Phosphate ester fluids are self-extinguishing under direct flame exposure, a non-negotiable requirement in aircraft, where fluid ignition from a line rupture near hot engine components presents catastrophic risk. The fluid operates across a temperature range from -54°C to 135°C and requires EPDM or butyl rubber seals throughout the aircraft hydraulic circuit due to the chemical incompatibility of phosphate esters with standard nitrile and fluorocarbon materials. 5. Hydraulic Fluids Used in Marine Applications Marine hydraulic systems on commercial vessels, offshore platforms, and workboats use hydraulic fluid to power steering systems, deck cranes, anchor windlasses, stabilizer fins, and hatch cover actuators at operating pressures from 1,500 psi to 4,000 psi. Vessels operating in environmentally protected waters (harbors, rivers, and coastal zones) specify biodegradable hydraulic fluid meeting VDMA 24568 or ISO 15380 Type HETG or HEES standards with biodegradability above 60% by OECD 301B testing. Seawater-resistant additives, including rust inhibitors and demulsifiers, are required in marine hydraulic fluid to prevent corrosion and water contamination in systems exposed to high humidity and salt spray environments. 6. Hydraulic Fluids Used in Construction Machinery Construction equipment hydraulic systems on excavators, wheel loaders, cranes, and articulated dump trucks operate on wide viscosity index mineral oil or multigrade hydraulic fluid at pressures from 3,500 psi to 5,000 psi across ambient temperatures from -20°C to 45°C. Main pump flow rates from 80 GPM to 150 GPM in 20-ton to 50-ton excavators require fluid with a viscosity index above 140 to maintain adequate film thickness at cold start without excessive thinning at peak operating temperature. Fluid change intervals on construction equipment typically range from 2,000 hours to 4,000 hours, with oil analysis sampling every 500 hours to monitor viscosity, contamination, and wear metal content before the scheduled drain interval. Hydraulic Fluids Used for Lubrication of System Components Hydraulic fluid lubricates pump pistons, valve spools, cylinder rods, and motor bearings by forming a hydrodynamic film of 1 to 10 micrometers between moving surfaces at relative velocities from 1 to 10 meters per second. Anti-wear additives containing zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDDP) at concentrations from 0.05% to 0.15% protect surfaces operating under boundary lubrication conditions at contact pressures from 50,000 psi to 200,000 psi at the asperity level inside axial piston pumps. Maintaining fluid viscosity above the minimum specification of 10 centistokes at maximum operating temperature preserves the lubricating film and prevents pump service life reduction from 10,000 hours to below 2,000 hours caused by metal-to-metal contact under collapsed film conditions. "As design engineers, we often focus so much on sizing heavy steel cylinders and selecting powerful pumps that we treat hydraulic fluid as an afterthought (just something you buy by the bucket to fill the circuit). But the reality is that fluid functions as a critical moving component within our assembly, squeezing through precision clearances as small as a human blood cell. If we do not explicitly design around how that fluid thins out under heat or chemically attacks our seals, even the most robust mechanical design on paper will fail catastrophically in the field." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering 8. Hydraulic Fluids Used for Heat Transfer and Cooling Hydraulic fluid removes heat generated by pressure drops across valves, internal pump and motor leakage, and mechanical friction by carrying thermal energy from the circuit back to the reservoir and heat exchanger for dissipation. A standard industrial hydraulic system generates heat at 20% to 30% of total input power, meaning a 50-horsepower system produces 10 to 15 horsepower of heat that the fluid must transport continuously to the cooling circuit. Fluid specific heat capacity from 1.67 to 2.09 kJ per kilogram per degree Celsius for mineral oils determines the volume of fluid required to absorb the heat load without exceeding the maximum operating temperature of 80°C to 90°C for petroleum-based grades in continuous duty operation. What Are the Advantages of Using Hydraulic Fluid? The advantages of using hydraulic fluid are listed below. High Power Density : Hydraulic fluid transmits forces from 1,000 pounds to over 5,000 tons through compact hoses and cylinders at pressures from 1,000 psi to 5,000 psi, achieving power density no pneumatic or mechanical system matches at equivalent component size. Simultaneous Lubrication : The same fluid that transmits power lubricates every internal moving surface it contacts, eliminating the need for separate lubrication systems in pumps, valves, and actuators. Effective Heat Dissipation: Hydraulic fluid carries thermal energy from pressure drops and pump friction to the reservoir and heat exchanger, maintaining system temperature below 60°C to 65°C across continuous duty cycles. Precise Controllability : Proportional flow control valves modulate fluid delivery to actuators continuously from 0 to maximum speed without discrete steps, enabling exact force and position control over loads from 50 pounds to thousands of tons. Overload Protection : Pressure relief valves preset from 500 psi to 5,000 psi divert excess fluid to the reservoir automatically when system load exceeds design limits, protecting all downstream components without operator intervention. Versatility Across Fluid Types : Petroleum-based, synthetic, biodegradable, water-based, and fire-resistant hydraulic fluid formulations cover operating environments from arctic construction sites to aircraft engine bays, making the hydraulic power transmission concept adaptable to nearly every industrial and mobile application. events.before: Resources / Machining Design / Ways to Save Money on CNC Prototypes Ways to Save Money on CNC Prototypes Written by Greg Paulsen 4 min read Published October 9, 2020 Updated October 30, 2026 CNC prototypes give you high-function, tight tolerance components that are ready to go out-of-the-box. These tips will help you shave costs off your next project. Sometimes parts need to be machined (instead of using other methods ), even if it’s a one-off prototype. This could be because of certain material requirements (e.g. PTFE, titanium, G-10 composite), tight tolerances, cosmetic finishes, or other needed attributes best made through CNC machining and turning services. CNC machining can be costly, but luckily, manufacturing platforms like Xometry can take on high-mix, low-volume work CNC jobs through a cost-effective network of machine job shops. Manufacturing networks offer the best value for prototype CNC manufacturing, delivering both low costs and short lead times. But beyond a high-quality manufacturer, what else can you do to save on your milled prototypes? Follow these four tips on prototyping, design, and supply chain best practices. Ask Yourself: Is it a Requirement or a Desirement? The number one cost driver for most prototype projects is scope creep . This is where the “nice-to-have” features are bundled in the same group as the “need-to-have” requirements. When structuring your prototype quote, a helpful phrase to ask yourself, your customer, or your engineers is: Is this a requirement or desirement ? Yes, “desirement” is a made up word, but it drives home the point that the goal of prototyping is to bring you to the next development step. Everything else, even if it will ultimately be part of the final product specification, is superfluous for your immediate success. Here are some common questions to ask yourself: Can I use the default tolerances on this part? Xometry’s manufacturing standards provide a generally acceptable manufacturing minimum for each process it offers. For CNC machining, this is +/- 0.005” for distance measurements. That’s about two sheets of paper’s thickness in total range. Specifying tighter tolerances on your Xometry quote will increase the part price slightly. The tighter the tolerance is, and the more tight tolerance areas there are, the more expensive your part will be. The nature of this pricing is a stack up, which will inflate the part price. Make sure to look at what is absolutely necessary for your prototype’s tolerances and only specify those to save costs. Do I need these cosmetics? Although features like laser engraving, silkscreen, and other part identification can be relatively low-cost in volume, their setup fees will have a significant impact on price and lead time at low quantities. If your CNC machined prototype is for function only, then you can probably opt out of the identification requirement. This consideration also applies to non-standard surface finishes, such as reduced surface roughness or post-process finishing services (discussed more below). Does this prototype need to be in the final material? Aluminum 6061 is the most commoditized metal for CNC machining and turning. This means that pricing will be lower for aluminum parts and the lead times are typically faster. Prototyping in aluminum 6061 can save costs and time compared to many other engineered alloys<dynamic-value> 7000-series aluminum or titanium. If your part is already destined for 6061 aluminum, then you are all set. You can use the Xometry Instant Quoting Engine℠ to easily see the pricing differences by toggling options for materials and alloys. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Simplify if Possible Many high-volume metal manufacturing methods such as die-casting can be prototyped using CNC machining. If possible, a die-cast design should have all drafts removed to dramatically reduce costs and machine time when CNC machining. This is because die casting design practices are similar to injection molding, requiring draft angles. A 3-degree draft across a series of features requires a milling process called surfacing, where a small mill moves in small increments to make a sloped feature. This can often more than double the price due to overhead time. By suppressing drafts, or minimizing the need to surface in general, you will get the same performance without added costs. A CNC machined prototype part Share Costs in Batches Xometry offers competitive pricing for one-off CNC machined parts. However, the per piece price will still dramatically decrease over even a few added quantities. This is because setups are shared between machined parts. When quoting for prototype milled parts, it is good practice to see what the price of adding 1 or 2 additional pieces will be by changing quantities—the price difference is often smaller than you think. Take Advantage of Xometry’s Speed and Tools The best part about Xometry’s online instant quoting site is its ease and transparency when pricing. You can choose from expedited, standard, or economy options for machined and turned parts. Pricing and lead times on quote automatically update based on applied quantities, features, tolerances, and finishing options. With Xometry, you have dedicated staff available to assist you in your choices and even help you get the most out of your budget. events.after: Resources / Machining Design / Ways to Save Money on CNC Prototypes Ways to Save Money on CNC Prototypes Written by Greg Paulsen 4 min read Published October 9, 2020 Updated October 30, 2026 CNC prototypes give you high-function, tight tolerance components that are ready to go out-of-the-box. These tips will help you shave costs off your next project. Sometimes parts need to be machined (instead of using other methods ), even if it’s a one-off prototype. This could be because of certain material requirements (e.g. PTFE, titanium, G-10 composite), tight tolerances, cosmetic finishes, or other needed attributes best made through CNC machining and turning services. CNC machining can be costly, but luckily, manufacturing platforms like Xometry can take on high-mix, low-volume work CNC jobs through a cost-effective network of machine job shops. Manufacturing networks offer the best value for prototype CNC manufacturing, delivering both low costs and short lead times. But beyond a high-quality manufacturer, what else can you do to save on your milled prototypes? Follow these four tips on prototyping, design, and supply chain best practices. Ask Yourself: Is it a Requirement or a Desirement? The number one cost driver for most prototype projects is scope creep . This is where the “nice-to-have” features are bundled in the same group as the “need-to-have” requirements. When structuring your prototype quote, a helpful phrase to ask yourself, your customer, or your engineers is: Is this a requirement or desirement ? Yes, “desirement” is a made up word, but it drives home the point that the goal of prototyping is to bring you to the next development step. Everything else, even if it will ultimately be part of the final product specification, is superfluous for your immediate success. Here are some common questions to ask yourself: Can I use the default tolerances on this part? Xometry’s manufacturing standards provide a generally acceptable manufacturing minimum for each process it offers. For CNC machining, this is +/- 0.005” for distance measurements. That’s about two sheets of paper’s thickness in total range. Specifying tighter tolerances on your Xometry quote will increase the part price slightly. The tighter the tolerance is, and the more tight tolerance areas there are, the more expensive your part will be. The nature of this pricing is a stack up, which will inflate the part price. Make sure to look at what is absolutely necessary for your prototype’s tolerances and only specify those to save costs. Do I need these cosmetics? Although features like laser engraving, silkscreen, and other part identification can be relatively low-cost in volume, their setup fees will have a significant impact on price and lead time at low quantities. If your CNC machined prototype is for function only, then you can probably opt out of the identification requirement. This consideration also applies to non-standard surface finishes, such as reduced surface roughness or post-process finishing services (discussed more below). Does this prototype need to be in the final material? Aluminum 6061 is the most commoditized metal for CNC machining and turning. This means that pricing will be lower for aluminum parts and the lead times are typically faster. Prototyping in aluminum 6061 can save costs and time compared to many other engineered alloys<dynamic-value> 7000-series aluminum or titanium. If your part is already destined for 6061 aluminum, then you are all set. You can use the Xometry Instant Quoting Engine℠ to easily see the pricing differences by toggling options for materials and alloys. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo Simplify if Possible Many high-volume metal manufacturing methods such as die-casting can be prototyped using CNC machining. If possible, a die-cast design should have all drafts removed to dramatically reduce costs and machine time when CNC machining. This is because die casting design practices are similar to injection molding, requiring draft angles. A 3-degree draft across a series of features requires a milling process called surfacing, where a small mill moves in small increments to make a sloped feature. This can often more than double the price due to overhead time. By suppressing drafts, or minimizing the need to surface in general, you will get the same performance without added costs. A CNC machined prototype part Share Costs in Batches Xometry offers competitive pricing for one-off CNC machined parts. However, the per piece price will still dramatically decrease over even a few added quantities. This is because setups are shared between machined parts. When quoting for prototype milled parts, it is good practice to see what the price of adding 1 or 2 additional pieces will be by changing quantities—the price difference is often smaller than you think.
