You can design the perfect gear profile, but if you do not control the furnace atmosphere, you risk brittle carbide networks at the roots or unpredictable quench distortion that throws your tolerances out the window. True design for manufacturing means modeling the case gradient as part of the mechanical system, not just treating heat treatment as a post-processing afterthought." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering What Equipment Is Used in Carburizing? The equipment that is used in the carburizing process is listed below. Controlled Atmosphere Furnaces: Sealed batch or continuous furnaces maintain precise hydrocarbon gas atmospheres at temperatures from 870°C to 930°C. Keeping all carburizing parameters, including temperature, carbon potential, and cycle time, under control is imperative to obtain a desired homogeneous carburizing case depth. Vacuum Furnaces: A vacuum furnace may be backfilled with a carburizing gas mixture after the load has been heated to the desired carburizing temperature, and vacuum furnaces are specifically suited for high-temperature carburizing. Quench Tanks: Oil quench tanks rapidly cool carburized parts from austenitizing temperature, freezing the high-carbon surface into martensite. High-pressure gas quenching is combined with vacuum carburizing, using quenching gas such as nitrogen or helium at 2 MPa, with quenching intensity controlled by gas pressure. Gas Delivery Systems: Precision flow control systems meter hydrocarbon feed gases (methane, propane, or acetylene) into the furnace chamber. The gas supply is modulated in accordance with the surface area of the part, helping to ensure that there are no uncarburized or over-carburized areas. Temperature Control Systems: Thermocouples and PID controllers maintain the furnace temperature within tight tolerances throughout the carburizing cycle. Temperature increases the diffusion rate, leading to a deeper case depth in less time than a case developed at a lower temperature. Carbon Potential Monitoring Equipment: Carbon control is critical to producing consistency in hardness, microstructure, and overall geometry. It is common practice to use in situ carbon probes to ensure proper control in achieving desired metallurgical results. How Do Furnaces Control Carbon Potential During Carburizing? Furnaces control carbon potential during carburizing by regulating the available carbon concentration at the steel surface. The furnace atmosphere supplies carbon through gases (methane, propane, carbon monoxide, or endothermic carrier gas). Oxygen probes, dew point sensors, and infrared gas analyzers monitor the atmosphere during the heat cycle. The control system adjusts gas flow to keep the carbon potential near the target surface carbon level. A high carbon potential increases carbon transfer, while excess carbon creates soot, retained austenite, or carbide networks. A low carbon potential reduces carbon absorption and produces shallow or uneven case depth. Temperature, soaking time, gas composition, and atmosphere circulation control the final carbon gradient. Accurate carbon potential control gives gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts a consistent hardened case after quenching. Stable atmosphere circulation helps maintain uniform carbon transfer across complex surfaces and deep gear teeth. Precise furnace control reduces case depth variation, surface defects, and post-quench hardness inconsistency. Does Quenching Occur After Carburizing? Yes, quenching occurs after carburizing because the carbon-enriched surface must transform into hard martensite. Carburizing raises the surface carbon level while the steel remains in the austenitic range. Rapid cooling locks carbon into the crystal structure and creates a hard, wear-resistant case. Oil, gas, or polymer quenching controls cooling speed depending on steel grade, part geometry, and distortion limits. The low-carbon core remains tougher than the hardened surface, which helps the part absorb impact and bending loads. Tempering usually follows quenching to reduce brittleness and stabilize hardness. Proper quench control reduces cracking, warping, and uneven hardness across the case. Cooling severity must match the part section size, alloy content, and required final hardness. Gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts rely on the hardened case produced by Quenching . What Are the Applications of Carburizing? The applications of carburizing are listed below. Automotive Gears: Automotive ring-and-pinion gears, truck transmission components, construction equipment drivetrains, and wind turbine gearbox stages all benefit from carburizing's combination of a deep hardened layer and tough core. Transmission Shafts: Transmission shafts carry torsional loads and require hard wear-resistant surfaces at spline interfaces and bearing journals while maintaining core ductility to resist shock loads during gear engagement. Bearings: Components (gears, camshafts, and bearings) commonly undergo carburizing to extend their service life under demanding conditions. Bearing races carburized to 58 to 62 HRC resist rolling contact fatigue across millions of load cycles in automotive and industrial service. Industrial Machine Components: Parts suitable for carburizing include bearings, bearing races, gears, and pinion shafts, which require a hard outer surface and a tough, fatigue-resistant core. Aerospace Drive Systems: Carburized parts offer superior fatigue performance and a more gradual hardness gradient than comparable induction-hardened parts. Heavy Equipment Wear Parts: Deep-case carburizing is essential for construction equipment with shock loads. Bucket teeth, track links, and drive sprockets on heavy machinery endure abrasive soil contact and impact, requiring deep carburized cases (up to 6.4 mm) for extended wear life. Why Is Carburizing Commonly Used for Gears and Bearings? Carburizing is commonly used for gears and bearings because the parts need hard, wear-resistant surfaces and impact-resistant cores. Gear teeth face sliding contact, rolling contact, and repeated load transfer during operation. Bearing surfaces face continuous pressure, friction, and fatigue stress from rolling elements or mating shafts. Carburizing creates a carbon-enriched martensitic case that resists pitting, scuffing, abrasion, and surface deformation. The lower carbon core stays tougher, which helps gears and bearings absorb shock loads without brittle fracture. Case depth control matters because shallow hardening wears too soon, while excessive case depth increases distortion risk. Quenching and tempering complete the process by setting surface hardness, reducing brittleness, and improving dimensional stability. Gearboxes, drivetrains, industrial machinery, and aerospace assemblies use carburized gears and bearings when long service life depends on strong surfaces and tough interiors. Proper carbon control helps gear teeth and bearing races maintain consistent hardness across contact zones. Uniform case hardening reduces early surface failure during repeated load cycles. Are Automotive Transmission Components Frequently Carburized? Yes, automotive transmission components are frequently carburized because gears, shafts, splines, and clutch hubs need hard wear-resistant surfaces with tough impact-resistant cores. Transmission gears face sliding contact, rolling contact, tooth bending stress, and repeated torque transfer during vehicle operation. Carburizing creates a hardened martensitic case that resists pitting, scuffing, abrasion, and surface deformation. The low-carbon core stays ductile enough to absorb shock loads from shifting, acceleration, and drivetrain vibration. Case depth control helps transmission parts maintain tooth strength without excessive distortion after quenching. Tempering reduces brittleness and improves dimensional stability after the hardening cycle. Automotive drivetrains use carburized components when long service life depends on surface durability and core toughness. How Does Carburizing Compare to Other Surface Hardening Processes? Carburizing compares to other surface hardening processes by adding carbon through diffusion at high austenitizing temperatures, while nitriding adds nitrogen at lower temperatures, induction hardening uses rapid localized heating, and carbonitriding adds carbon plus nitrogen. Carburizing produces a deep hardened case after quenching, making the process suitable for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts. Nitriding forms a hard nitride layer without quenching, which reduces distortion and works well for wear-resistant precision parts. Induction hardening changes the surface microstructure through electromagnetic heating and quenching, but it does not add carbon or nitrogen to the steel. Carbonitriding uses a carbon and nitrogen-rich atmosphere at lower temperatures than carburizing, producing a thinner case with good wear resistance. Carburizing gives deeper case depth than nitriding and carbonitriding in many gear and shaft applications. Nitriding gives strong surface hardness with low distortion because the process temperature stays below the austenitizing range. Induction hardening works fastest for selective areas (gear teeth, bearing journals, and shaft shoulders). Carbonitriding suits small parts, fasteners, stampings, and low-carbon steel components needing a shallow hardened case. Process choice depends on required case depth, distortion limits, steel grade, surface hardness, production volume, and final part function. What Is the Difference Between Carburizing and Nitriding? The difference between carburizing and nitriding is that carburizing diffuses carbon into steel, while nitriding introduces nitrogen to form hard nitrides at the surface. Carburizing uses austenitizing temperatures and quenching to transform the carbon-enriched case into hard martensite. Nitriding uses lower temperatures and forms hard nitride compounds without a required quench. Carburizing produces deeper case depths for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts that need high load capacity. Nitriding creates a thinner, very hard surface layer with lower distortion risk for precision parts. Carburizing suits low-carbon steels that need a tough core and wear-resistant surface. Nitriding suits alloy steels with nitride-forming elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum, and vanadium). Carburizing is chosen when heavy contact loads require deeper hardened support under the surface. Nitriding is chosen when dimensional stability and reduced distortion matter after final machining. Is Carburizing Deeper Than Induction Hardening? Yes, carburizing is deeper than induction hardening because carbon diffusion creates a hardened case below the steel surface. Carburizing case depth is controlled by temperature, carbon potential, and holding time. Induction hardening heats the surface rapidly through electromagnetic energy, then quenching hardens the heated layer. Induction hardening depth depends on frequency, power, heating time, and steel hardenability. Carburizing suits gears, shafts, and bearings that need deeper support under heavy contact loads. Induction hardening suits localized areas (shaft journals, gear teeth, and bearing seats) when fast surface hardening and reduced heat exposure matter. Case depth selection depends on load, wear pattern, geometry, distortion limits, and final performance requirements. Carburized cases give gradual hardness support below the surface, which helps resist subsurface fatigue under repeated rolling contact. Induction-hardened layers offer faster processing, but hardened depth remains more limited by heating pattern and frequency control. What Are the Limitations of Carburizing? The limitations of Carburizing are distortion risk, long processing times, dimensional changes, and limited suitability for certain alloys. High carburizing temperatures and quenching create thermal gradients, phase changes, and residual stress that shift precision features from final dimensions. Gear teeth, bearing races, shafts, and splines need post-heat treatment inspection because carburizing changes part size and shape. Carburizing takes longer than induction hardening or carbonitriding because carbon must diffuse into the steel surface over time. Process time increases when deeper case depth is required, depending on temperature and holding time. High-carbon steels and tool steels are poor candidates because excess surface carbon raises the risk of carbide networks, retained austenite, cracking, and unstable hardness. Low-carbon alloy steels remain better choices when parts need a hard case and tough core. Post-carburizing grinding or finishing becomes necessary when tight tolerances or surface finish requirements matter. Process control must account for furnace atmosphere, quench medium, part geometry, and alloy response before production approval. Why Can Carburizing Cause Distortion in Steel Parts? Carburizing distorts steel parts because high-temperature exposure and quenching create thermal stresses, phase changes, and dimensional movement. The part expands during heating, then contracts unevenly during cooling. Quenching cools thin sections faster than thick sections, which creates uneven stress across the part. Austenite transforms into martensite during rapid cooling, and the volume change shifts the final dimensions. Gears, shafts, splines, and bearing races are sensitive because precise surfaces move under heat treatment stress. Sharp corners, uneven wall thickness, and complex shapes increase distortion risk during quenching. Controlled heating, uniform fixturing, proper quench selection, and post-treatment grinding reduce dimensional variation after carburizing. Residual stresses remain after quenching when different sections cool and transform at different rates. Distortion control requires part-specific fixtures, balanced geometry, controlled quench agitation, and inspection after heat treatment. Can Excessive Carburizing Increase Brittleness? Yes, excessive carburizing increases brittleness. Case depths that are too deep lead to through carburizing of the tooth, resulting in loss of ductility and reduced fatigue life. Quench embrittlement negatively affects the relationship between hardness to ultimate tensile strength, especially at high hardness and elevated steel carbon levels. The plastic portion of the stress-strain curve is reduced or eliminated, causing the steel to fail in a brittle manner. Tempering at 300°F to 400°F reduces brittleness while preserving hardness, strength, compressive residual stress, and fatigue life. Controlling carbon potential and case depth within specified limits is mandatory to prevent brittleness while retaining the fatigue and wear performance gains that carburizing delivers. Excess carbon creates carbide networks that interrupt the hardened case structure and reduce impact resistance. Metallurgical inspection verifies surface carbon level, effective case depth, and hardness profile before the part enters service. events.after: Resources / Materials / Carburizing: Definition, Process, and Applications Carburizing: Definition, Process, and Applications Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 24 min read Published July 16, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Carburizing is a thermochemical heat treatment process that introduces carbon into the surface layer of low-carbon steel, raising the surface carbon concentration to produce a hardened, wear-resistant outer case while preserving a tough and ductile core. Carburizing is defined as a heat treatment process, per AGMA 923, in which austenitized steel contacts a carbonaceous atmosphere with enough carbon potential. Carbon-bearing gases adsorb at the steel surface, dissociate, and diffuse inward to create a carbon concentration gradient. The metallurgical outcome relies on carbon diffusion into austenitized steel, followed by quenching to form a hardened martensitic surface layer. Industrial applications span automotive drivetrains, aerospace drive systems, transmission shafts, gears, bearings, and precision-machined components where surface durability and core toughness must coexist. Carburizing is a process whereby carbon is diffused into the surface of steel at high temperatures, where austenite is present, and the diffusion rate of carbon is reasonably high. Case carburizing steels are widely used in applications where high surface hardness is required in combination with good core toughness, high strength, and fatigue resistance. The depth of the hardened layer, known as the effective case depth (ECD), is controlled by temperature, carbon potential, and time in the furnace. Carburizing, quenching, and tempering increase surface hardness, wear resistance, fatigue strength, and tensile strength while producing the desired compressive residual stress at the surface. What Is Carburizing? Carburizing is a heat treatment process that diffuses carbon into the surface of steel at elevated temperatures to improve surface hardness and wear resistance. The process is commonly applied to low-carbon steels because the base metal needs a hard outer layer and a tough interior core. Carbon enters the steel surface during austenitizing, then moves inward through diffusion to create a controlled carbon concentration gradient. Quenching transforms the carbon-enriched surface into hardened martensite, which improves resistance against wear, pitting, and contact fatigue. Tempering follows quenching to reduce brittleness and stabilize the hardened case. Gears, shafts, bearings, pins, and drivetrain components use carburizing when surfaces face repeated friction, impact, or rolling contact. The core remains lower in carbon, which helps the part absorb shock without cracking under service loads. Carburized steel parts combine a hard case with a ductile core, making the process suitable for high-load mechanical components. Process control depends on carbon potential, temperature, holding time, quench medium, and required case depth. Why Does Carbon Increase Steel Hardness? Carbon increases steel hardness because higher carbon content promotes martensite formation during quenching. Austenitized steel dissolves carbon in the face-centered cubic structure before rapid cooling. Quenching traps carbon inside the body-centered tetragonal martensite structure, creating lattice strain that resists deformation. Higher carbon content increases the hardness of the martensitic case because the distorted crystal structure blocks dislocation movement. Wear resistance improves because the hardened surface resists abrasion, indentation, and rolling contact damage. Carburizing uses the effect by enriching the surface carbon level while keeping the core lower in carbon and tougher. Tempering follows quenching to reduce brittleness while keeping useful surface hardness for gears, shafts, bearings, and pins. Added carbon raises hardenability at the surface, so the treated case responds better to rapid cooling. The hardened case supports contact loads better because the carbon-enriched martensite resists plastic deformation. Excess carbon requires control because retained austenite or carbide networks reduce dimensional stability and toughness. Does Carburizing Harden the Entire Metal Component? Gas carburizing works by heating low-carbon steel in a furnace with a controlled carbon-rich atmosphere, then diffusing carbon into the steel surface. Methane, propane, natural gas, or endothermic carrier gas supplies carbon to the furnace atmosphere. The steel enters the austenitic temperature range, where the surface absorbs carbon-bearing gases. The gases dissociate at the surface, allowing carbon atoms to diffuse inward and form a carbon concentration gradient. Furnace carbon potential, temperature, and holding time control case depth and surface carbon level. Quenching follows carburizing to transform the carbon-enriched surface into hard martensite. Tempering reduces brittleness while keeping the wear-resistant case needed for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts. Gas carburizing gives manufacturers consistent case hardening for a metal component that needs high surface durability and a tougher core. How Does the Carburizing Process Work? Vacuum carburizing differs from conventional carburizing because it uses a low-pressure furnace environment instead of a standard atmospheric furnace. The process introduces hydrocarbon gases (acetylene or propane) in controlled pulses at low pressure. Carbon diffuses into the steel surface under cleaner conditions because the furnace contains little oxygen and reduced gas contamination. The cleaner environment reduces oxidation, soot formation, and intergranular surface attack compared with conventional gas carburizing. Low-pressure control improves repeatability because temperature, pressure, gas flow, and boost diffusion cycles are closely regulated. Vacuum carburizing gives better case depth control for gears, shafts, bearings, fuel system parts, and aerospace components. The process needs precise quenching control because distortion risk still depends on part geometry, steel grade, and cooling severity. High-pressure gas quenching is commonly paired with vacuum carburizing to reduce oil contamination and improve part cleanliness. Complex parts benefit from vacuum carburizing when blind holes, narrow channels, or deep gear teeth require uniform carbon delivery. What Happens During Carbon Diffusion in Steel? During carbon diffusion in steel, carbon atoms migrate into the steel surface at elevated temperatures through atomic movement inside austenite. The steel surface absorbs carbon from a carbon-rich atmosphere, then carbon atoms move from the high-carbon surface into the lower-carbon interior. The movement creates a carbon concentration gradient, with the highest carbon level near the surface and a lower carbon level deeper in the part. Temperature increases atomic mobility, so carbon diffusion becomes faster inside the austenitic structure. Holding time controls how far carbon travels into the steel, which sets the final case depth. Quenching follows diffusion and transforms the carbon-enriched surface into hard martensite. The lower carbon core remains tougher, giving carburized parts a hard, wear-resistant case with a ductile interior. Longer diffusion time produces a deeper hardened case when temperature and carbon potential remain controlled. Excess surface carbon requires control because carbide networks or retained austenite reduce toughness and dimensional stability. Why Is Austenitizing Necessary Before Carburizing? Austenitizing is necessary before carburizing because steel must enter the austenitic structure to absorb and diffuse carbon effectively. Austenite has higher carbon solubility than ferrite, which allows carbon atoms to move into the surface during heat treatment. The elevated temperature increases atomic movement and helps create a controlled carbon concentration gradient. Carbon diffusion becomes limited when steel stays below the austenitizing range. Quenching after carburizing transforms the carbon-enriched austenite into hard martensite at the surface. The lower carbon core remains tougher, giving the part a hard case and ductile interior. Proper austenitizing improves case depth control by preparing the steel structure for uniform carbon movement. Insufficient austenitizing creates uneven carbon diffusion, which leads to inconsistent hardness after quenching. Controlled temperature and soak time help maintain the required balance from hardened surface to tough core. What Are the Main Types of Carburizing Processes? The main types of carburizing processes are listed below. Gas Carburizing: Gas carburizing is a surface chemistry process that improves the case depth hardness of a component by diffusing carbon into the surface layer to improve wear and fatigue resistance, using a gaseous carbon-rich atmosphere. The process runs at temperatures from 870°C to 930°C with hydrocarbons (methane or propane) as the carbon source, making it cost-effective for high-volume production. Pack Carburizing: Pack carburizing uses charcoal or carbon-containing powder sealed in a box, with the temperature range for carburizing at 870°C to 930°C. Carbon reacts with ambient air to form carbon dioxide and then carbon monoxide, which delivers carbon to the steel surface. Liquid Carburizing: Liquid carburizing is performed in salt baths (sodium cyanide), producing uniform surfaces and reducing oxide formation. The process is suited for small batches requiring consistent surface treatment across complex geometries. Vacuum Carburizing: The low-pressure carburizing (LPC) process takes place in a temperature range from 870°C to 1050°C with a pressure range from 5 mbar to 15 mbar, and during the complete process, the treated components are not exposed to any traces of oxygen. Plasma Carburizing: Plasma carburizing requires high equipment costs and is restricted to special carburizing treatments, such as those of parts having deep holes. The process uses ionized gas to deliver carbon to the steel surface under controlled electrical discharge conditions. How Does Gas Carburizing Work? Tempering reduces brittleness while keeping the wear-resistant case needed for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts. Gas carburizing gives manufacturers consistent case hardening for steel components that need high surface durability and a tougher core. Process control keeps the carbon profile uniform across gear teeth, shaft shoulders, and bearing surfaces. Atmosphere monitoring prevents excess carbon pickup that leads to retained austenite, carbide networks, or dimensional instability. How Does Vacuum Carburizing Differ From Conventional Carburizing? The process needs precise quenching control because distortion risk depends on part geometry, steel grade, and cooling severity. High-pressure gas quenching is commonly paired with vacuum carburizing to reduce oil contamination and improve part cleanliness. Complex geometries benefit from vacuum carburizing when blind holes, narrow channels, or deep gear teeth require controlled carbon delivery. Is Pack Carburizing One of the Oldest Carburizing Methods? Yes, pack carburizing is one of the oldest carburizing methods because it uses solid carbon materials to add carbon to steel surfaces. The process places low-carbon steel parts inside a sealed container filled with charcoal, coke, or carbon-rich powder. Heat causes carbon monoxide to form inside the pack, which reacts at the steel surface and supplies carbon for diffusion. The steel absorbs carbon at elevated temperatures, then develops a hardened case after quenching. Pack carburizing needs longer cycle times than gas or vacuum carburizing because carbon transfer and temperature control are slower. The method remains useful for simple parts, low-volume work, repair operations, and cases where advanced furnace atmosphere control is not required. What Materials Are Commonly Carburized? The materials that are commonly carburized are listed below. Low-Carbon Steels: Carburizing is performed on low-carbon steel at high temperatures where austenite is present, as the diffusion rate of carbon is reasonably high under those conditions. Steels with 0.10% to 0.25% carbon are the most frequently carburized, as they retain ductile cores after quenching. Alloy Steels: Alloy steels with manganese, chromium, and molybdenum additions respond well to carburizing because the alloying elements improve hardenability and support deeper martensitic transformation during quenching. Gear Steels: Carburizing is a widely used, effective technique to increase surface hardness of steel used in gears and achieve compressive residual stress, which contributes to long life and cost-effective production. Nickel-Chromium Steels: SAE 9310 steel, a high-nickel steel, is typically used in aircraft industry applications and other demanding applications, with nickel content improving core toughness and fatigue strength after carburizing and quenching. Chromium-Molybdenum Steels: Chromium-molybdenum steels (4118 or 8620) are carburized in aerospace and heavy equipment applications where high-strength cores combined with hard surfaces are required for drive components and shafts. Why Are Low-Carbon Steels Commonly Used for Carburizing? Low-carbon steels are commonly used for carburizing because they keep a ductile core while developing a hardened surface after carburizing and quenching. The low-carbon core absorbs impact and bending loads without cracking easily. Carbon enrichment increases surface carbon content, which allows martensite formation during quenching. The hardened case improves wear resistance, indentation resistance, and contact fatigue performance. The toughness difference from surface to core makes low-carbon steel suitable for gears, shafts, bearings, pins, and drivetrain parts. Medium-carbon or high-carbon steels already contain more carbon, so carburizing offers less benefit and higher distortion risk. Low-carbon steel gives manufacturers a practical balance of machinability, case hardness, and core toughness. The process allows parts to be machined before heat treatment, then hardened at the surface after final shaping. Alloying elements in low-carbon steels (nickel, chromium, and molybdenum) improve hardenability and support deeper case performance. Can High-Carbon Steels Be Carburized Effectively? No, high-carbon steels are not carburized effectively because they already contain enough carbon for hardening. Carburizing adds surface carbon, which increases the risk of excessive hardness, retained austenite, carbide networks, cracking, and distortion after quenching. High-carbon steel hardens through standard heat treatment without needing extra carbon diffusion at the surface. The process gives limited benefit when the core and surface already have high carbon content. Low-carbon steels remain the preferred choice because carburizing creates a hard case while preserving a tougher core. High-carbon steels suit through-hardening applications better than case hardening. Excess carbon at the surface makes quench response harder to control during final heat treatment. Tool steels and bearing steels usually need controlled hardening and tempering rather than added carbon diffusion. What Mechanical Properties Change During Carburizing? The mechanical properties that change during carburizing are listed below. Surface Hardness Increase: The results are increased surface hardness, wear resistance, fatigue strength, and localized case yield strength through carburizing and quenching plus tempering, as well as the desired compressive residual stress on the surface. Improved Wear Resistance: Gas carburizing improves the case depth hardness of a component by diffusing carbon into the surface layer to improve wear and fatigue resistance. The hardened martensitic case resists abrasion and rolling contact fatigue under repetitive loading. Improved Fatigue Strength: Carburizing is used to enhance fatigue resistance and toughness properties of dynamically loaded components. Compressive residual stresses in the case counteract tensile fatigue stresses during cyclic loading, extending the component's service life. Tough Core Retention: The core remains relatively soft and tough after quenching. Tempering is performed to increase the toughness and ductility of the quenched part. Higher Contact Stress Resistance: Carburizing is a widely used, effective technique to increase surface hardness of steel and achieve compressive residual stress, contributing to long life and cost-effective production. The hardened case supports high contact pressures in gear mesh and bearing race applications without surface yielding How Does Carburizing Improve Wear Resistance? Carburizing improves wear resistance by forming a hardened martensitic surface layer that resists abrasion, rolling contact fatigue, and surface deformation. Carbon diffusion raises the surface carbon level before quenching, which allows the outer case to transform into hard martensite. The hardened case resists scratching, pitting, scuffing, and indentation during sliding or rolling contact. The tougher low-carbon core supports impact loads without making the entire part is brittle. Gears, shafts, bearings, cams, and pins benefit from the hard case because the contact surface carries repeated friction and pressure. Tempering after quenching reduces brittleness while keeping the surface hardness needed for long service life. The hardened surface reduces material loss when parts move against mating components under load. The carbon-enriched case delays crack initiation on surfaces exposed to repeated contact stress. The core maintains toughness, so carburized parts resist sudden fracture better than through-hardened parts. Does Carburizing Improve Fatigue Life? Yes, carburizing improves fatigue life by creating a hard carbon-enriched case that resists surface crack initiation under repeated loading. The hardened martensitic surface reduces pitting, indentation, and rolling contact damage on gears, shafts, bearings, and cams. Compressive residual stress at the surface helps slow crack growth during cyclic service. The tougher core supports impact and bending loads without making the entire component brittle. Proper case depth, quench control, and tempering improve fatigue performance by balancing hardness with dimensional stability. Carburized parts gain longer service life when surface contact stress and repeated load cycles control failure risk. A uniform carbon gradient reduces weak transition zones from the hardened case to the core. Controlled tempering improves fatigue behavior by reducing quench stress while keeping surface hardness. Controlled Atmosphere Furnaces: Sealed batch or continuous furnaces maintain precise hydrocarbon gas atmospheres at temperatures from 870°C to 930°C. Keeping all carburizing parameters, including temperature, carbon potential, and cycle time, under control is imperative to obtain a desired homogeneous carburizing case depth. Vacuum Furnaces: A vacuum furnace may be backfilled with a carburizing gas mixture after the load has been heated to the desired carburizing temperature, and vacuum furnaces are specifically suited for high-temperature carburizing. Quench Tanks: Oil quench tanks rapidly cool carburized parts from austenitizing temperature, freezing the high-carbon surface into martensite. High-pressure gas quenching is combined with vacuum carburizing, using quenching gas such as nitrogen or helium at 2 MPa, with quenching intensity controlled by gas pressure. Gas Delivery Systems: Precision flow control systems meter hydrocarbon feed gases (methane, propane, or acetylene) into the furnace chamber. The gas supply is modulated in accordance with the surface area of the part, helping to ensure that there are no uncarburized or over-carburized areas. Temperature Control Systems: Thermocouples and PID controllers maintain the furnace temperature within tight tolerances throughout the carburizing cycle. Temperature increases the diffusion rate, leading to a deeper case depth in less time than a case developed at a lower temperature. Carbon Potential Monitoring Equipment: Carbon control is critical to producing consistency in hardness, microstructure, and overall geometry. It is common practice to use in situ carbon probes to ensure proper control in achieving desired metallurgical results. How Do Furnaces Control Carbon Potential During Carburizing? Furnaces control carbon potential during carburizing by regulating the available carbon concentration at the steel surface. The furnace atmosphere supplies carbon through gases (methane, propane, carbon monoxide, or endothermic carrier gas). Oxygen probes, dew point sensors, and infrared gas analyzers monitor the atmosphere during the heat cycle. The control system adjusts gas flow to keep the carbon potential near the target surface carbon level. A high carbon potential increases carbon transfer, while excess carbon creates soot, retained austenite, or carbide networks. A low carbon potential reduces carbon absorption and produces shallow or uneven case depth. Temperature, soaking time, gas composition, and atmosphere circulation control the final carbon gradient. Accurate carbon potential control gives gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts a consistent hardened case after quenching. Stable atmosphere circulation helps maintain uniform carbon transfer across complex surfaces and deep gear teeth. Precise furnace control reduces case depth variation, surface defects, and post-quench hardness inconsistency. Does Quenching Occur After Carburizing? Yes, quenching occurs after carburizing because the carbon-enriched surface must transform into hard martensite. Carburizing raises the surface carbon level while the steel remains in the austenitic range. Rapid cooling locks carbon into the crystal structure and creates a hard, wear-resistant case. Oil, gas, or polymer quenching controls cooling speed depending on steel grade, part geometry, and distortion limits. The low-carbon core remains tougher than the hardened surface, which helps the part absorb impact and bending loads. Tempering usually follows quenching to reduce brittleness and stabilize hardness. Proper quench control reduces cracking, warping, and uneven hardness across the case. Cooling severity must match the part section size, alloy content, and required final hardness. Gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts rely on the hardened case produced by Quenching . What Are the Applications of Carburizing? The applications of carburizing are listed below. Automotive Gears: Automotive ring-and-pinion gears, truck transmission components, construction equipment drivetrains, and wind turbine gearbox stages all benefit from carburizing's combination of a deep hardened layer and tough core. Transmission Shafts: Transmission shafts carry torsional loads and require hard wear-resistant surfaces at spline interfaces and bearing journals while maintaining core ductility to resist shock loads during gear engagement. Bearings: Components (gears, camshafts, and bearings) commonly undergo carburizing to extend their service life under demanding conditions. Bearing races carburized to 58 to 62 HRC resist rolling contact fatigue across millions of load cycles in automotive and industrial service. Industrial Machine Components: Parts suitable for carburizing include bearings, bearing races, gears, and pinion shafts, which require a hard outer surface and a tough, fatigue-resistant core. Aerospace Drive Systems: Carburized parts offer superior fatigue performance and a more gradual hardness gradient than comparable induction-hardened parts. Heavy Equipment Wear Parts: Deep-case carburizing is essential for construction equipment with shock loads. Bucket teeth, track links, and drive sprockets on heavy machinery endure abrasive soil contact and impact, requiring deep carburized cases (up to 6.4 mm) for extended wear life. Why Is Carburizing Commonly Used for Gears and Bearings? Carburizing is commonly used for gears and bearings because the parts need hard, wear-resistant surfaces and impact-resistant cores. Gear teeth face sliding contact, rolling contact, and repeated load transfer during operation. Bearing surfaces face continuous pressure, friction, and fatigue stress from rolling elements or mating shafts. Carburizing creates a carbon-enriched martensitic case that resists pitting, scuffing, abrasion, and surface deformation. The lower carbon core stays tougher, which helps gears and bearings absorb shock loads without brittle fracture. Case depth control matters because shallow hardening wears too soon, while excessive case depth increases distortion risk. Quenching and tempering complete the process by setting surface hardness, reducing brittleness, and improving dimensional stability. Gearboxes, drivetrains, industrial machinery, and aerospace assemblies use carburized gears and bearings when long service life depends on strong surfaces and tough interiors. Proper carbon control helps gear teeth and bearing races maintain consistent hardness across contact zones. Uniform case hardening reduces early surface failure during repeated load cycles. Are Automotive Transmission Components Frequently Carburized? Yes, automotive transmission components are frequently carburized because gears, shafts, splines, and clutch hubs need hard wear-resistant surfaces with tough impact-resistant cores. Transmission gears face sliding contact, rolling contact, tooth bending stress, and repeated torque transfer during vehicle operation. Carburizing creates a hardened martensitic case that resists pitting, scuffing, abrasion, and surface deformation. The low-carbon core stays ductile enough to absorb shock loads from shifting, acceleration, and drivetrain vibration. Case depth control helps transmission parts maintain tooth strength without excessive distortion after quenching. Tempering reduces brittleness and improves dimensional stability after the hardening cycle. Automotive drivetrains use carburized components when long service life depends on surface durability and core toughness. How Does Carburizing Compare to Other Surface Hardening Processes? Carburizing produces deeper case depths for gears, shafts, bearings, and drivetrain parts that need high load capacity. Nitriding creates a thinner, very hard surface layer with lower distortion risk for precision parts. Carburizing suits low-carbon steels that need a tough core and wear-resistant surface. Nitriding suits alloy steels with nitride-forming elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum, and vanadium). Carburizing is chosen when heavy contact loads require deeper hardened support under the surface. Nitriding is chosen when dimensional stability and reduced distortion matter after final machining. Is Carburizing Deeper Than Induction Hardening? Yes, carburizing is deeper than induction hardening because carbon diffusion creates a hardened case below the steel surface. Carburizing case depth is controlled by temperature, carbon potential, and holding time. Induction hardening heats the surface rapidly through electromagnetic energy, then quenching hardens the heated layer. Induction hardening depth depends on frequency, power, heating time, and steel hardenability. Carburizing suits gears, shafts, and bearings that need deeper support under heavy contact loads. Induction hardening suits localized areas (shaft journals, gear teeth, and bearing seats) when fast surface hardening and reduced heat exposure matter. Case depth selection depends on load, wear pattern, geometry, distortion limits, and final performance requirements. Carburized cases give gradual hardness support below the surface, which helps resist subsurface fatigue under repeated rolling contact. Induction-hardened layers offer faster processing, but hardened depth remains more limited by heating pattern and frequency control. What Are the Limitations of Carburizing? The limitations of Carburizing are distortion risk, long processing times, dimensional changes, and limited suitability for certain alloys. High carburizing temperatures and quenching create thermal gradients, phase changes, and residual stress that shift precision features from final dimensions. Gear teeth, bearing races, shafts, and splines need post-heat treatment inspection because carburizing changes part size and shape. Carburizing takes longer than induction hardening or carbonitriding because carbon must diffuse into the steel surface over time. Process time increases when deeper case depth is required, depending on temperature and holding time. High-carbon steels and tool steels are poor candidates because excess surface carbon raises the risk of carbide networks, retained austenite, cracking, and unstable hardness. Low-carbon alloy steels remain better choices when parts need a hard case and tough core. Post-carburizing grinding or finishing becomes necessary when tight tolerances or surface finish requirements matter. Process control must account for furnace atmosphere, quench medium, part geometry, and alloy response before production approval. Why Can Carburizing Cause Distortion in Steel Parts? Carburizing distorts steel parts because high-temperature exposure and quenching create thermal stresses, phase changes, and dimensional movement. The part expands during heating, then contracts unevenly during cooling. Quenching cools thin sections faster than thick sections, which creates uneven stress across the part. Austenite transforms into martensite during rapid cooling, and the volume change shifts the final dimensions. Gears, shafts, splines, and bearing races are sensitive because precise surfaces move under heat treatment stress. Sharp corners, uneven wall thickness, and complex shapes increase distortion risk during quenching. Controlled heating, uniform fixturing, proper quench selection, and post-treatment grinding reduce dimensional variation after carburizing. Residual stresses remain after quenching when different sections cool and transform at different rates. Distortion control requires part-specific fixtures, balanced geometry, controlled quench agitation, and inspection after heat treatment. Can Excessive Carburizing Increase Brittleness? Yes, excessive carburizing increases brittleness. Case depths that are too deep lead to through carburizing of the tooth, resulting in loss of ductility and reduced fatigue life. Quench embrittlement negatively affects the relationship between hardness to ultimate tensile strength, especially at high hardness and elevated steel carbon levels. The plastic portion of the stress-strain curve is reduced or eliminated, causing the steel to fail in a brittle manner. Tempering at 300°F to 400°F reduces brittleness while preserving hardness, strength, compressive residual stress, and fatigue life. Controlling carbon potential and case depth within specified limits is mandatory to prevent brittleness while retaining the fatigue and wear performance gains that carburizing delivers. Excess carbon creates carbide networks that interrupt the hardened case structure and reduce impact resistance. Metallurgical inspection verifies surface carbon level, effective case depth, and hardness profile before the part enters service. events.before: Resources / Materials / Edge Crush Test: Definition, How It Works, Advantages, and Challenges Edge Crush Test: Definition, How It Works, Advantages, and Challenges Written by Dean McClements 13 min read Published February 8, 2024 Updated October 30, 2026 The edge crush test (ECT) is a codified international test methodology. It is used in the packaging industry to assess the strength and durability of corrugated or paperboard materials and others. The ECT determines the maximum compressive loading a corrugated material can withstand on its edge, before the onset of collapse. This quantifies the material's resistance to being crushed when pressure is applied along its edge. This can only be loosely interpolated in the strength of finished structures, but it provides a consistent measure across various materials that informs in this regard. This article will discuss what the edge crush test is and how it works. The advantages and challenges will also be covered. What Is the Edge Crush Test (ECT)? The ECT is a generally accepted testing method employed in the packaging industry to evaluate the strength and resilience of corrugated or paperboard materials. ECT determines a material's capacity to withstand edge loading forces, simulating the stresses experienced during stacking and transportation. Why Is the Edge Crush Test Important? The edge crush test ensures that samples of packaging materials meet specific strength standards, guaranteeing the reliability and integrity of resultant packaging. It helps in selecting appropriate materials. It also ensures they can withstand typical and extreme stacking and handling stresses, and safeguarding the enclosed products from damage. ECT results aid in designing efficient and cost-minimized packaging solutions by avoiding over-engineering by assuming minimal material strength. Using materials with the appropriate ECT values reduces excessive material/resource usage, reducing environmental impact in materials sourcing and disposal. Efficient packaging design also minimizes shipping volumes, reducing transport impact. The ECT promotes consistency in packaging quality and performance, by providing cross-application knowledge and consistency in materials performance understanding. How Does ECT Work? The ECT is a rigorous and highly repeatable test that informs deeply about a single aspect of material strength, with profound influence on real-world packaging performance. A small, rectangular specimen of the material is cut and conditioned to a specified humidity and temperature to ensure consistent test conditions. The conditioned specimen is placed vertically between two rigid platens on a testing machine. The specimen's edges are aligned with the platens, ensuring a secure fit. A steadily increasing compressive force is applied to the specimen's edge at a constant rate using the testing machine. The force is applied until the material buckles or collapses, identified by any sudden motion in response to increased loading. The maximum force applied before the material's edge failure is recorded as the edge crush test result. How Much Force Does the Edge Crush Testing Require? The force required during an ECT depends on various factors such as: the specific material being tested, its thickness, and the testing conditions. ECT is typically conducted following standardized preparation defined by organizations like the International Safe Transit Association (ISTA) and the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM). A steadily increasing compressive force is applied to the clamped specimen's edge until it buckles or collapses. The force at which this failure occurs is recorded as the ECT value in lbf/in or kN/m. The measured force required varies widely with material type and thickness, but it is typically within the range of 10–60 lbf/in or 0.6–3.4 kN/m. It can exceed this range, depending on the material's type, thickness, and composition. What Are the Advantages of the Edge Crush Test? The ECT offers various enabling advantages in the packaging industry such as: Provides an accurate measure of a material's resistance to edge compression, assisting designers and manufacturers in selecting appropriate packaging materials for specific products. Ensures consistency in material assessment and facilitates reliable comparisons between divergent materials. Helps in the design and execution of sufficient but minimal packaging that can withstand real-world stacking and transportation stresses. This reduces material overuse while ensuring the safety and integrity of enclosed products during transit. Assists in cost-minimized packaging design, avoiding over-engineering resulting from otherwise common underestimation of the material capability. Optimized material selection based on ECT results in reduced resource usage and footprint of packaging solutions. Serves as a batch/sample evaluation quality-control tool, ensuring that packaging materials meet or exceed specified strength standards, reducing the risk of package strength variations over time. How Is the Edge Crush Test Performed? The ECT is performed following standardized procedures: Cut a rectangular specimen of the to-be-tested material to the required dimensions. The sample should be conditioned to standardized temperature and humidity conditions to ensure consistent testing, compensating for the variability of card materials with changes in humidity and temperature. Place the conditioned specimen vertically between the rigid platens of the ECT machine, with edges aligned precisely with the platens to ensure a secure fit. Initiate the test by applying progressively increasing compressive force to the specimen's edge at a constant ramp rate, as specified by the testing standard. This rate applies until the material's edge buckles or collapses. Record the maximum force applied to the specimen's edge before failure occurs. This recorded force (in lbf/in or kN/m), is the edge crush test value. Use the recorded ECT value to assess the material's strength and suitability for various packaging applications, helping determine its resistance to edge compression. Experience is required in the interpretation of the ECT result as a driver of design considerations and material choices. What Do Edge Crush Test Values Indicate? ECT values indicate the strength and resistance of corrugated cardboard or paperboard materials to edge compression. ECT values quantify how much compressive force a material can withstand along its edge before it collapses or buckles. They help assess the ability of packaging materials—and therefore package designs—to support the weight of stacked packages. Where stacking strength is crucial, higher values are achieved by alternate material selection and by increased thickness or other material-specification alterations. ECT values assist in defining the structural integrity of packaging during transportation and storage, resulting in packaging that maintains its shape and protects the enclosed products. How Does ECT Compare to Other Strength Tests? ECT is one of several standardized tests used in the packaging industry to assess the strength (and other performance aspects) of packaging materials. Each test method has its focus and measures different aspects of material strength. The ECT measures a material's resistance to edge compression, simulating the stresses encountered during stacking. Burst strength (Mullen test), for example, assesses a material's resistance to puncture or bursting. It measures the force required to puncture a material with a blunt object. A compression test evaluates a finished package's ability to withstand vertical loads and uniform compression during storage or transportation. Tensile tests, on the other hand, assess the material's ability to withstand linear tensile forces. They are used to evaluate the tensile strength and elongation properties of materials. An ECT is more relevant for packaging materials in applications in which stacking strength is crucial, while burst strength is more relevant when puncture resistance is a primary concern. Both compression and edge crush tests provide different insights into packaging performance, with compression tests assessing the overall package's load-bearing capacity. As a rule, a good understanding of the interpretation of ECT results will inform the design process and materials selection and lead to a successful execution that can be evaluated by compression testing. While tensile tests provide valuable information about material properties, an ECT is more relevant for understanding how corrugated materials perform under stacking and handling conditions. As a rule, packaging structures are used in compressive loading scenarios, so tensile resilience is a minor factor in most applications. What Are the Edge Crush Test Standards and Regulations? ECT corrugated testing is standardized by several organizations and testing bodies. These organizations ensure consistency and reliability in the evaluation of the strength of corrugated cardboard, paperboard, and other packaging materials. Some standards and regulations are: TAPPI T 811: Provides procedures for conducting the ECT on corrugated fiberboard. ISO 3037: Specifies a method for determining the edgewise compressive strength of corrugated fiberboard. ISTA 3A: Evaluates the strength and performance of packaging materials and systems. FEFCO Standard 8: Determines the ECT of corrugated cardboard. While the tests do not provide directly interchangeable/comparable results, the interpretation between them is well understood and most manufacturers of materials will be able to specify their materials’ performance expectations under various test scenarios/standards. What Device Does an Edge Crush Test Use? ECT corrugated testing is typically conducted using a specialized testing machine known as an edge crush tester or ECT tester. These devices consist of: Sample Holder: Holds the corrugated cardboard or paperboard specimen securely in a vertical position during the test. Platens: Two rigid, flat platens are used to apply the compressive force to the specimen's edge. One platen is stationary, while the other is moved by a hydraulic or screw system. Load Cell: This is used to measure the force applied to the specimen and record the maximum force at the point of failure/collapse. Control Panel: The control panel allows operators to set testing parameters, such as loading rate and test duration, and monitor the test progress/outcome. How Is the ECT Performed on Different Materials? An ECT can be performed on various materials, but it is most commonly used for corrugated cardboard and paperboard materials in the packaging industry. The testing procedure remains consistent regardless of the material being tested, the primary focus being evaluating the material's resistance to edge compression. The ECT is extensively used for corrugated cardboard, of which it assesses the strength and stacking performance of different weights/constructions—single-wall, double-wall, and triple-wall corrugated. Note that “single wall” is two skins and one corrugation layer . It is also applied to paperboard materials, including solid bleached sulfate (SBS), solid unbleached sulfate (SUS), and folding carton board, to determine the same key property. In some cases, the ECT may be adapted for testing non-paper-based materials like plastic corrugated sheets or fiber-reinforced composites. However, the applicability and relevance of ECT to these materials may vary, and alternative testing methods can be more appropriate. A typical single-wall corrugated card will range from 32 ECT to 44 ECT, defining the normal range for performance, the upper value being 44 lbf/in material performance. A box constructed from a typical double-wall corrugated board might achieve a 48 lbf/in material ECT value, often resulting in ECT box values of 44 ECT to 50 ECT in some cases. What ISO Standard Applies to the ECT? The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) provides a standard for the edge crush test (ECT) by non-waxed edge testing. Specifically, ISO 3037 is the ISO standard that defines the method for determining the edgewise compressive strength of corrugated fiberboard. What Are the Challenges and Limitations of Edge Crush Testing? Challenges and limitations of the ECT include: Variations in material composition, structure, and manufacturing processes can greatly impact ECT results. Small differences in material properties result in significant variations in test outcomes. The ECT typically tests small specimens of material, which may be poorly representative of the entire packaging structure. Many materials exhibit anisotropic behavior, meaning their strength properties can vary in different directions. An ECT primarily assesses the material's resistance to edge compression, which may not capture anisotropic characteristics, as a standard end-on corrugation orientation is not equivalent to an edge-on presentation. This influence is greatly reduced in multi-layer materials. The moisture content of corrugated materials can greatly influence ECT results. Surface conditions, such as coatings or treatments, can impact ECT results. Testing should consider the surface properties of the material, ideally testing coated and uncoated samples for clarity. The ECT measures material strength in a controlled laboratory setting, which will not necessarily replicate the complex conditions experienced during shipping and handling. The ECT is primarily intended for corrugated cardboard and paperboard materials. It may not be ideally suited to assessing the strength of other materials used in packaging. What Are Real World Applications of the Edge Crush Test? The ECT is widely applied as a reference point in the packaging industry to evaluate the stacking strength and edge compression resistance of widely employed materials. Some real-world applications are: ECT helps packaging professionals choose the most appropriate materials for packaging applications, ensuring that packaging can withstand the stacking pressures and handling stresses to be encountered. Test results inform the design and structural integrity of packaging solutions. Designers use ECT data to develop packaging that protects products efficiently and minimizes the risk of damage. Manufacturers and suppliers use the ECT to maintain assurance of consistent material quality, confirming the meeting or exceeding of specified strength standards, reducing the risk of subsequent and potentially expensive packaging failures. The ECT assists in optimizing packaging materials, minimizing the over-application of resources, and contributing to a reduced footprint for packaging solutions. The ECT is particularly important in industries like consumer electronics, in which fragile and extremely high-value items must be protected during shipping and handling. In the food and beverage supply chain, the ECT helps reduce the storage and transportation risks of organic contaminants from damaged products. Is the ECT Only Used for Corrugated Cardboard Materials? ECT is primarily designed for assessing the strength and stacking performance of corrugated cardboard and paperboard materials. However, the ECT is not limited exclusively to corrugated paper/card materials. It can potentially be adapted or used as a reference test method for other materials in specific applications for which edge compression resistance is a relevant factor. This adaptation may require alterations to testing procedures or equipment to suit the characteristics of the material being tested. While the ECT is highly applicable to corrugated materials, other materials may have their standardized testing methods or criteria for assessing their strength and performance in different contexts. What Is the Difference Between an ECT and an Impact Test? The two test regimes are complementary but quite different in approach. Their mode of stress application differs by 90°; so edge crush testing evaluates the performance of the sheet edge in load bearing, whereas an impact test evaluates the ability of the material’s face to withstand impact. Both tests have high applicability in packaging design, and it is common for packaging designers to reference these and other factors in selecting material type, thickness, and orientation in real-world solutions. Summary This article presented the edge crush test, explained it, and discussed how it works and its various advantages. To learn more about the edge crush test, contact a Xometry representative . The ECT assists in optimizing packaging materials, minimizing the over-application of resources, and contributing to a reduced footprint for packaging solutions. The ECT is particularly important in industries like consumer electronics, in which fragile and extremely high-value items must be protected during shipping and handling. In the food and beverage supply chain, the ECT helps reduce the storage and transportation risks of organic contaminants from damaged products. Is the ECT Only Used for Corrugated Cardboard Materials? ECT is primarily designed for assessing the strength and stacking performance of corrugated cardboard and paperboard materials. However, the ECT is not limited exclusively to corrugated paper/card materials. It can potentially be adapted or used as a reference test method for other materials in specific applications for which edge compression resistance is a relevant factor. This adaptation may require alterations to testing procedures or equipment to suit the characteristics of the material being tested. While the ECT is highly applicable to corrugated materials, other materials may have their standardized testing methods or criteria for assessing their strength and performance in different contexts. What Is the Difference Between an ECT and an Impact Test? The two test regimes are complementary but quite different in approach. Their mode of stress application differs by 90°; so edge crush testing evaluates the performance of the sheet edge in load bearing, whereas an impact test evaluates the ability of the material’s face to withstand impact. Both tests have high applicability in packaging design, and it is common for packaging designers to reference these and other factors in selecting material type, thickness, and orientation in real-world solutions.
