events.before: Resources / Materials / Sulfur (S): Formula, Element and Uses Sulfur (S): Formula, Element and Uses Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 24 min read Published June 10, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Sulfur (S) is a bright yellow, nonmetallic chemical element with the atomic number 16 and the chemical symbol S, occurring abundantly in nature as elemental deposits near volcanic regions and as sulfide and sulfate minerals throughout Earth's crust. Sulfur (S) ranks among the most industrially significant nonmetals, serving as the foundational raw material for sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), the most widely produced industrial chemical globally, with annual production exceeding 270 million metric tons. The element's chemical reactivity, low cost, and availability drive its application across fertilizer manufacturing, rubber vulcanization, petroleum refining, pharmaceuticals, and surface treatment processes. Sulfur connects to metal processing through sulfuric acid anodizing, where H₂SO₄ acts as the electrolyte to form protective oxide layers on aluminum surfaces, improving corrosion and wear resistance. In metallurgy, controlled sulfur additions to steel and nickel alloys form manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions that improve machinability by promoting chip breakage during cutting operations, a property exploited in free-machining grades (12L14 steel, Monel 405). Sulfur's interactions with steel types and grades, nickel alloys, and surface treatment chemistry establish it as a chemically active element with consequences across manufacturing, agriculture, energy, and materials engineering. What Is Sulfur (S)? Sulfur (S) is a chemical element found in minerals and industrial materials, classified as a nonmetal with atomic number 16, atomic mass 32.06 u, and the chemical symbol S. In its elemental form, sulfur is a bright yellow, brittle solid at room temperature, odorless when pure but producing the characteristic pungent smell of hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) or sulfur dioxide (SO₂) when burned or reduced. Sulfur ranks as the 10th most abundant element in the universe and the 5th most abundant element on Earth by mass, occurring in volcanic deposits, evaporite minerals (gypsum, anhydrite), and sulfide ores (pyrite, galena, cinnabar). The element is the starting material for sulfuric acid production, the world's most consumed industrial chemical. Sulfur participates in the biological amino acids cysteine and methionine, making it an essential element for all living organisms. In industrial contexts, sulfur drives chemical manufacturing, rubber processing, fertilizer production, and metallurgical applications across dozens of sectors. The smell of sulfur, in its pure elemental form, is essentially odorless at room temperature. The strong, unpleasant smell commonly associated with sulfur comes from sulfur compounds, primarily hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), which produces an odor resembling rotten eggs at concentrations as low as 0.5 parts per billion (ppb), and sulfur dioxide (SO₂), which emits a sharp, pungent, choking odor at concentrations above 1 ppm. What Is the Chemical Formula of Sulfur (S)? The chemical formula of Sulfur is represented by the symbol S as a single element, but in its most stable naturally occurring molecular form, it exists as S₈, a crown-shaped ring of eight covalently bonded sulfur atoms. The S₈ molecule, known as cyclooctasulfur or orthorhombic sulfur, is the thermodynamically stable allotrope of sulfur at room temperature and standard pressure. Each sulfur atom in the S₈ ring forms two covalent bonds with adjacent sulfur atoms, completing its valence shell without forming double bonds in the ring structure. Sulfur also exists in other allotropic forms: S₆ (rhombohedral sulfur), S₁₂, and polymeric sulfur (plastic sulfur), a chain-like amorphous form produced by quenching molten sulfur in cold water. In chemical compounds, sulfur appears in formulas including H₂SO₄ (sulfuric acid), H₂S (hydrogen sulfide), SO₂ (sulfur dioxide), and Na₂SO₄ (sodium sulfate), each reflecting sulfur's variable oxidation states from -2 to +6. What Is Sulfur (S) as a Chemical Element? Sulfur is a nonmetallic chemical element in Group 16 (chalcogens) of the periodic table, Period 3, with the atomic number 16 and the standard atomic weight of 32.06 u. The element has an electronegativity of 2.58 on the Pauling scale, a value reflecting its moderate tendency to attract electrons in covalent bonds, placing it below oxygen (3.44) and above carbon (2.55). Sulfur has four naturally occurring stable isotopes: sulfur-32 (94.93%), sulfur-33 (0.76%), sulfur-34 (4.29%), and sulfur-36 (0.02%), with sulfur-32 dominating natural abundance. The electron configuration of sulfur is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴, providing six valence electrons that drive its chemical bonding in compounds ranging from sulfides (-2 oxidation state) to sulfates (+6 oxidation state). Sulfur melts at 115.2°C and boils at 444.6°C, properties that make it processable at relatively low temperatures compared to metals, supporting its use in chemical manufacturing and vulcanization processes. Is Sulfur a Metal or Nonmetal? Sulfur is a nonmetal, and its physical and chemical properties confirm the classification across every relevant criterion. At room temperature, sulfur is a brittle, yellow solid that fractures when struck, lacking the malleability and ductility characteristic of metals. Sulfur's electrical conductivity is extremely low at approximately 10⁻¹⁵ S/m, making it an electrical insulator rather than a conductor. Thermal conductivity measures 0.205 W/(m·K), far below the values of metals (iron: 80 W/(m·K), copper: 400 W/(m·K)). Sulfur does not exhibit metallic luster; its surface is dull and matte yellow. Chemically, sulfur gains electrons (acts as an oxidizing agent) instead of donating them, a behavior opposite to metals. The combination of brittleness, non-conductivity, low thermal conductivity, and electron-gaining behavior classifies sulfur unambiguously as a nonmetal. How Is Sulfuric Acid Anodizing Connected to Sulfur Chemistry? Sulfuric acid anodizing is connected to sulfur-based compounds, specifically sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), as the electrolyte solution that drives the electrochemical formation of a protective aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) layer on aluminum surfaces, connecting sulfur chemistry directly to metal surface engineering. In the anodizing process, aluminum parts are immersed in a sulfuric acid bath with concentrations from 15% to 20% H₂SO₄ by weight, at temperatures from 18°C to 22°C, and a direct current is applied at voltage levels from 12 V to 21 V. The sulfuric acid provides the ionic conductivity needed to sustain the electrochemical reaction, where oxygen ions generated at the anode react with the aluminum surface to grow a porous Al₂O₃ film from 5 µm to 25 µm thick. Sulfur incorporates into the oxide film as sulfate ions, typically comprising 12% to 15% of the layer by weight, and is the chemically active component of the electrolyte that governs film growth rate, porosity, and thickness. Xometry's surface finishing services include sulfuric acid anodizing for aluminum components requiring improved corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and decorative finish quality. How Is Sulfuric Acid Used in Anodizing Processes? Sulfuric acid is used in anodizing processes as the primary electrolyte in Type II (standard) and Type III (hard coat), providing the ionic medium through which electrical current flows and aluminum oxide grows on the workpiece surface. A 15% to 20% H₂SO₄ solution at 18°C to 22°C and 12 V to 21 V produces an oxide layer from 5 µm to 25 µm thick with moderate porosity in Type II anodizing, suitable for dyeing and corrosion protection in architectural and consumer applications. Higher H₂SO₄ concentrations (up to 25%) combined with lower temperatures (0°C to 5°C) and higher voltages (25 V to 100 V) produce denser oxide layers from 25 µm to 100 µm thick in Type III hard coat anodizing, with hardness from 400 HV to 600 HV, suitable for wear-resistant military, aerospace, and industrial components. The sulfuric acid electrolyte simultaneously drives oxide growth at the barrier layer and partially dissolves the outer porous layer, controlling the equilibrium between oxide formation and dissolution that determines final film thickness and structure. Is Sulfuric Acid Anodizing Used to Improve Metal Corrosion Resistance? Yes, sulfuric acid anodizing is used to improve metal corrosion resistance by converting the aluminum surface into a thick, stable aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) layer that acts as a physical barrier preventing moisture, oxygen, and corrosive agents from reaching the underlying metal. The anodized Al₂O₃ layer produced in sulfuric acid electrolyte is integral to the aluminum surface, growing both inward and outward from the original metal surface, and does not peel or delaminate like applied coatings. Salt spray testing (ASTM B117) confirms that Type II anodized aluminum withstands 336 hours to 500 hours of salt fog without corrosion failure, while Type III hard coat anodized surfaces exceed 1,000 hours. Sealing the anodized layer in hot water (96°C to 100°C) or nickel acetate solution closes the pores, further improving corrosion resistance by preventing electrolyte penetration into the oxide structure. How Does Sulfur Interact With Steel Types and Grades? Sulfur interacts with steel types and grades through its role as an impurity that affects the steel’s properties. Sulfur is added in controlled amounts to specific steel grades to improve machinability through the formation of manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions, soft non-metallic particles that act as internal lubricants and chip breakers during cutting operations, reducing tool wear and improving surface finish. Sulfur content ranges from 0.08% to 0.35% by weight in free-machining steels, well above the residual sulfur levels below 0.05% maintained in structural and high-strength steel grades. MnS inclusions form when manganese reacts with sulfur during solidification, precipitating as elongated particles oriented in the rolling direction of the steel bar or plate. The elongated MnS particles disrupt the continuity of the steel matrix in the machining zone, promoting chip breakage and reducing cutting forces by 15% to 30% compared to equivalent low-sulfur grades. Excess sulfur above the specified range reduces transverse toughness, ductility, and weldability, requiring careful composition control in free-machining steel types and grades . How Does Sulfur Affect 4140 Alloy Steel? Sulfur affects 4140 alloy steel, improving machinability by forming MnS inclusions that act as chip breakers during turning, milling, and drilling operations, reducing cutting forces and extending tool life in high-volume machining environments. Standard 4140 steel (AISI/SAE specification) contains sulfur as a residual element limited to a maximum of 0.040% by weight, a level low enough to preserve toughness, fatigue resistance, and weldability while permitting minor machinability benefits. Free-machining variants of 4140 incorporate sulfur from 0.08% to 0.13%, producing a measurable increase in machinability rating from approximately 55% to 70% of the AISI 1212 baseline. The tradeoff of elevated sulfur in 4140 is a reduction in Charpy impact toughness in the transverse direction, where MnS inclusions act as crack initiation sites. Xometry's CNC machining services process 4140 alloy steel in standard and free-machining variants, with material selection guided by the balance of machinability to the mechanical performance required for each component. How Does Sulfur Affect 1020 Carbon Steel? Sulfur affects 1020 carbon steel, improving machinability through MnS inclusion formation, with standard 1020 (AISI/SAE) containing sulfur limited to a maximum of 0.050% and free-machining 1215 steel (a sulfur-enhanced low-carbon grade) containing 0.26% to 0.35% sulfur for maximum cutting efficiency. The machinability rating of low-carbon steel increases significantly; 12L14 (leaded, sulfurized) reaches a machinability rating of 170% relative to the AISI 1212 baseline at sulfur levels from 0.26% to 0.35%, while 1215 (sulfurized, non-leaded) achieves 136%. The MnS inclusions in sulfurized 1020-class steels reduce cutting tool temperature by acting as a solid lubricant at the tool-chip interface, lowering crater wear rates on carbide and high-speed steel tooling. Elevated sulfur in low-carbon grades reduces weldability and cold-forming performance, limiting free-machining sulfurized steels to machined-only applications where subsequent welding or forming is not required, especially in 1020 carbon steel . How Does Sulfur Affect Stainless Steel? Sulfur affects stainless steel, improving machinability but reducing corrosion resistance, requiring precise composition control to balance cutting performance against the corrosion protection that defines the material's primary function. Standard austenitic grades (304, 316) limit sulfur to a maximum of 0.030% to preserve the integrity of the passive Cr₂O₃ film; MnS inclusions at higher sulfur levels act as initiation sites for pitting corrosion in chloride environments, where sulfide inclusions dissolve preferentially and create corrosion pits in the surrounding matrix. Grade 303 stainless steel is the primary free-machining austenitic variant, containing 0.15% minimum sulfur, a level that dramatically improves machinability (approximately 78% of the AISI 1212 baseline, versus 45% for 304) at the cost of reduced pitting and crevice corrosion resistance relative to 304. The balance from machinability to corrosion resistance in sulfur-controlled stainless steel grades is governed by the intended service environment and the severity of corrosive exposure. Does Sulfur Improve Machinability in Different Steel Grades? Yes, sulfur improves machinability in different steel grades by forming manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions that reduce cutting forces, promote chip breakage, and decrease tool wear during turning, milling, drilling, and threading operations. The machinability improvement is quantified by the AISI machinability rating system, where 1212 steel (0.70% to 1.00% Mn, 0.16% to 0.23% S ) serves as the 100% baseline. Grades with increasing sulfur content show proportional machinability gains: 1215 (0.26% to 0.35% S) achieves 136%, 12L14 (sulfur plus lead) reaches 170%, and 303 stainless (0.15% min S) achieves 78% versus 304's 45%. The machinability benefit of sulfur applies across low-carbon, medium-carbon, alloy, and stainless steel categories, making sulfur the most cost-effective machinability additive in steel composition design. What Is the Role of Sulfur in Nickel Alloys? The role of Sulfur in nickel alloys is added in controlled amounts to specific free-machining grades to improve machinability through sulfide inclusion formation, while in standard structural nickel alloys, sulfur is treated as a harmful impurity limited to trace levels below 0.010% due to its severe embrittling effect on nickel at elevated temperatures. Nickel is highly susceptible to sulfur embrittlement; sulfur forms nickel sulfide (Ni₃S₂) at grain boundaries in nickel-rich alloys, a compound that melts at 637°C and creates liquid-phase grain boundary films that cause hot cracking during welding and hot working at temperatures above 600°C. Sulfur is balanced against manganese content to promote MnS formation rather than Ni₃S₂ in free-machining nickel alloy grades, directing sulfur into benign nickel-copper sulfide inclusions that aid chip breakage without causing grain boundary embrittlement. Xometry's manufacturing network processes nickel alloys across free-machining and standard grades, with sulfur content specified according to the mechanical and machinability requirements of each application. How Is Sulfur Related to Monel 405? Sulfur is related to Monel 405 at levels from 0.025% to 0.060% by weight to improve machinability, distinguishing grade 405 from Monel 400, which contains residual sulfur below 0.024% and offers superior corrosion resistance but lower machinability. Monel 405 is a nickel-copper alloy (approximately 63% to 70% Ni, 28% to 34% Cu) where the sulfur addition promotes sulfide inclusion formation that aids chip formation during turning, drilling, and threading on automatic screw machines. The controlled sulfur content in Monel 405 raises its machinability rating to approximately 30% of the AISI 1212 baseline, compared to Monel 400's 22%, a meaningful improvement for high-volume machined parts. Sulfur content in Monel 405 is kept within the 0.025% to 0.060% range to ensure nickel-copper sulfide inclusions form preferentially over nickel sulfides, avoiding grain boundary embrittlement while delivering the machinability benefit that defines the grade. How Is Sulfur Related to Post Transition Metal Alloys? Sulfur in post-transition metal alloys (alloys based on elements including aluminum, lead, tin, bismuth, and indium) acts as an impurity or a deliberate additive that influences machinability and mechanical properties, depending on the specific alloy system and sulfur concentration. In aluminum alloys, sulfur is not a common additive; it appears as trace contamination at levels below 0.001%, with negligible effect on mechanical properties at the concentrations encountered in standard production. Sulfur interacts with lead and tin to form sulfide phases that influence solidification microstructure and casting surface quality in lead-based free-machining alloys and tin-bronze casting alloys. The effects of sulfur in post-transition metal alloys are alloy-system specific, requiring composition-dependent assessment rather than a universal characterization, as sulfur's role shifts from beneficial machinability additive to harmful impurity depending on the base metal's affinity for sulfide formation. Is Monel 405 a Nickel-Copper Alloy That Contains Controlled Sulfur Levels? Yes, Monel 405 is a nickel-copper alloy that contains controlled sulfur levels from 0.025% to 0.060% by weight, a compositional feature that defines the grade's identity as the free-machining variant of the Monel 400 family. The base composition of Monel 405 is nickel from 63% to 70% and copper from 28% to 34%, with the sulfur addition as the primary differentiating variable from Monel 400. Controlled sulfur in Monel 405 produces sulfide inclusions that break chips during automatic screw machine operations, enabling the manufacture of fittings, valve stems, and precision fasteners at production rates impractical with standard Monel 400. The sulfur range of 0.025% to 0.060% is tightly specified in ASTM B164 (standard specification for Monel rod, bar, and wire) to ensure consistent machinability without compromising corrosion resistance beyond acceptable limits for moderate service environments, making it suitable for applications where machinability is essential without sacrificing the key properties of Monel 405 . What Are the Uses of Sulfur? The uses of Sulfur are listed below. Production of Sulfuric Acid : Sulfur is the primary raw material for sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) synthesis via the Contact process, with over 270 million metric tons of H₂SO₄ produced globally each year. Fertilizer Manufacturing : Sulfur and sulfuric acid are used to produce ammonium sulfate, superphosphate, and other sulfur-containing fertilizers that supply essential nutrients to crops. Rubber Vulcanization : Sulfur crosslinks polymer chains in natural and synthetic rubber during vulcanization, converting soft, tacky rubber into durable, elastic material with tensile strength from 15 MPa to 30 MPa. Matches, Fireworks, and Gunpowder : Sulfur serves as a fuel component in black powder (10% sulfur) and as an ignition component in match heads and pyrotechnic compositions. Pesticides and Fungicides : Elemental sulfur and sulfur compounds are applied as fungicides and acaricides in agriculture, effective against powdery mildew, rust, and spider mites at application rates from 1 kg/ha to 5 kg/ha. Pharmaceuticals and Medicines : Sulfur compounds appear in antibiotics (sulfonamides), antifungal treatments (selenium sulfide), and topical acne medications containing sulfur from 3% to 10% concentration. Petroleum Refining : Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) removes sulfur compounds from crude oil fractions, producing recovered elemental sulfur as a byproduct while reducing sulfur in fuels to below 10 ppm to meet emission standards. Detergents and Chemical Products : Sulfonation reactions using SO₃ or H₂SO₄ produce sulfonate surfactants (linear alkylbenzene sulfonate, sodium lauryl sulfate) that form the active cleaning agents in laundry detergents, shampoos, and industrial cleaners. Solid design for manufacturing always looks past the screen to balance structural performance with actual machining costs." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering 1. Sulfur Used for Production of Sulfuric Acid Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) production is the largest single use of sulfur globally, consuming approximately 90% of elemental sulfur produced each year, with global H₂SO₄ output exceeding 270 million metric tons annually. The Contact process converts elemental sulfur into sulfuric acid through three sequential reactions: combustion of sulfur to sulfur dioxide (S + O₂ → SO₂), catalytic oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ over vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) catalyst at temperatures from 400°C to 600°C (2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃), and absorption of SO₃ in concentrated H₂SO₄ to produce oleum (H₂S₂O₇), which is then diluted with water to the target acid concentration. The double absorption Contact process achieves SO₂ conversion efficiencies above 99.7%, minimizing atmospheric SO₂ emissions while maximizing acid yield. Sulfuric acid produced from sulfur serves as the feedstock for fertilizer manufacturing (phosphoric acid, ammonium sulfate), petroleum refining (alkylation), metal processing (pickling, anodizing), battery acid (lead-acid batteries), and dozens of chemical synthesis pathways across nearly every industrial sector. 2. Sulfur Used for Fertilizer Manufacturing Sulfur and sulfuric acid are fundamental to fertilizer manufacturing, supplying both the sulfur nutrient required by plants and the acidifying agent needed to convert phosphate rock into water-soluble plant-available phosphate fertilizers. Superphosphate fertilizer is produced by reacting phosphate rock (Ca₃(PO₄)₂) with sulfuric acid to produce calcium dihydrogen phosphate (Ca(H₂PO₄)₂) and calcium sulfate (gypsum), with single superphosphate containing approximately 20% P₂O₅ and triple superphosphate reaching 44% to 48% P₂O₅. Ammonium sulfate ((NH₄)₂SO₄) fertilizer, containing 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur, is produced from sulfuric acid and ammonia and provides both macronutrients in a single product. Elemental sulfur applied directly to alkaline soils acidifies the root zone through bacterial oxidation to H₂SO₄ (by Thiobacillus bacteria), improving nutrient availability in high-pH soils. Global sulfur consumption in fertilizer production exceeds 50 million metric tons annually, reflecting agriculture's dependence on sulfur chemistry to maintain crop yields. Sulfur Used for Rubber Vulcanization Sulfur vulcanization converts natural rubber (polyisoprene) and synthetic rubbers (SBR, NBR, EPDM) from soft, thermoplastic materials into durable, elastic solids by forming covalent sulfur crosslinks from 1 to 8 sulfur atoms long, connecting adjacent polymer chains. Charles Goodyear discovered sulfur vulcanization in 1839, observing that heating rubber with sulfur at temperatures from 140°C to 180°C produced a material with dramatically improved mechanical properties, temperature stability, and resistance to solvent swelling. Sulfur loading in rubber compounds ranges from 0.5 parts per hundred rubber (phr) for efficient vulcanization systems to 30 phr to 50 phr for hard rubber (ebonite), which is fully crosslinked and rigid. Vulcanized rubber with 1 phr to 3 phr sulfur produces soft elastic products (gloves, balloons, foam) with tensile strength from 15 MPa to 25 MPa and elongation at break from 500% to 800%. Tire compounds use sulfur from 1.5 phr to 3.5 phr combined with accelerators (CBS, MBT) and activators (zinc oxide, stearic acid) to achieve the crosslink density required for tread wear, flex fatigue resistance, and heat buildup control in service. 4. Sulfur Used for Matches, Fireworks, and Gunpowder Sulfur serves as a fuel and combustion-modifier component in pyrotechnic compositions, contributing to ignition sensitivity, burn rate, and energy output in matches, fireworks, and black powder. Black powder (gunpowder) contains approximately 75% potassium nitrate (KNO₃), 15% charcoal, and 10% sulfur by weight; sulfur lowers the ignition temperature of the mixture, acts as a fuel, and reacts with potassium nitrate to produce potassium sulfide and release energy at a controlled rate suitable for propellant and pyrotechnic applications. Match heads in strike-anywhere matches contain sulfur compounds (antimony trisulfide, Sb₂S₃) combined with oxidizers and friction-sensitive materials that ignite at temperatures from 180°C to 230°C. In fireworks compositions, sulfur is incorporated into lift charges, burst charges, and color-producing stars, where its role as a reducing fuel complements oxidizers like potassium perchlorate (KClO₄) and potassium nitrate to sustain combustion at temperatures from 1,500°C to 2,000°C, producing the visual and auditory effects of aerial pyrotechnics. 5. Sulfur Used for Pesticides and Fungicides Elemental sulfur is one of the oldest and most widely used agricultural pesticides, applied as a fungicide, acaricide (miticide), and insecticide against a broad range of plant pathogens and arthropod pests at application rates from 1 kg/ha to 10 kg/ha, depending on crop and pest pressure. Sulfur controls fungal diseases, including powdery mildew (Erysiphe spp.), rust (Puccinia spp.), and scab (Venturia inaequalis) on grapes, stone fruits, and vegetables through direct contact toxicity, where sulfur vapor at the leaf surface inhibits fungal spore germination and disrupts cellular respiration in the pathogen. Wettable sulfur and sulfur dust formulations with particle sizes from 3 µm to 10 µm provide maximum surface coverage and fungicidal activity on crop foliage. Lime sulfur (calcium polysulfide, CaS₅) is a liquid formulation used as a dormant spray on fruit trees, controlling overwintering fungal inoculum and scale insects at dilutions from 1:10 to 1:50 in water. Sulfur-based pesticides are approved for organic agriculture under USDA National Organic Program (NOP) standards, making sulfur one of the few broad-spectrum pest control agents compatible with certified organic production systems. 6. Sulfur Used for Pharmaceuticals and Medicines Sulfur and sulfur-containing compounds appear across a wide range of pharmaceutical applications, from topical dermatological treatments to systemic antibiotics, reflecting sulfur's biological reactivity and its presence in amino acids essential to protein structure. Elemental sulfur in concentrations from 3% to 10% is used in topical acne treatments, where it acts as a keratolytic agent that breaks down excess keratin, reduces sebaceous gland activity, and exhibits mild antibacterial properties against Cutibacterium acnes. Sulfonamide antibiotics (sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine) contain a sulfonamide group (-SO₂-NH₂) that inhibits bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate synthesis in susceptible bacteria at minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) from 1 µg/mL to 64 µg/mL. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, (CH₃)₂SO) is used as a pharmaceutical carrier and anti-inflammatory agent, with FDA approval for treatment of interstitial cystitis at a 50% concentration instilled directly into the bladder. Selenium sulfide (SeS₂), a sulfur-containing compound, is the active ingredient in medicated shampoos for dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis at concentrations from 1% to 2.5%. Sulfur Used for Petroleum Refining Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) is the primary petroleum refining process that removes sulfur-containing compounds from crude oil fractions, converting organosulfur compounds (thiophenes, benzothiophenes, mercaptans) to hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) and sulfur-free hydrocarbons over cobalt-molybdenum or nickel-molybdenum catalysts at temperatures from 300°C to 400°C and hydrogen pressures from 3 MPa to 13 MPa. The recovered H₂S is converted to elemental sulfur via the Claus process, making petroleum refining the world's largest single source of recovered elemental sulfur, accounting for approximately 80% of global sulfur supply. Ultra-low sulfur diesel (ULSD) regulations in the United States and European Union require sulfur content below 15 ppm and 10 ppm, respectively, driving extensive HDS capacity in modern refineries. The removal of sulfur from petroleum products reduces SO₂ emissions from combustion engines, protects catalytic converters from sulfur poisoning, and meets air quality standards that limit atmospheric SO₂ concentrations to protect human health and reduce acid rain formation. 8. Sulfur Used for Detergents and Chemical Products Sulfonation reactions using sulfur trioxide (SO₃) or oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) introduce sulfonate groups (-SO₃H) into organic molecules, producing surfactants that form the active cleaning agents in laundry detergents, dishwashing liquids, shampoos, and industrial cleaners. Linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS), produced by sulfonating linear alkylbenzene with SO₃ at temperatures from 40°C to 60°C, is the most widely produced surfactant globally, with annual production exceeding 3 million metric tons. Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), produced by reacting lauryl alcohol with SO₃ or chlorosulfuric acid, is the primary surfactant in shampoos, toothpastes, and personal care products at concentrations from 5% to 30%. Sulfosuccinate surfactants (dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, DOSS) are used as wetting agents and emulsifiers in pharmaceutical formulations, food processing, and industrial applications. The sulfonate group's hydrophilic character (water-attracting) combined with the hydrophobic carbon chain of the parent molecule creates the amphiphilic structure responsible for surfactant cleaning action, making sulfur chemistry the foundation of the global detergent industry. What Are the Advantages of Using Sulfur? The advantages of using Sulfur are listed below. Abundant and Low Cost : Sulfur is among the most abundant elements on Earth and is recovered as a byproduct of petroleum refining and natural gas processing, making it one of the lowest-cost industrial raw materials at commodity prices from [$30 to $150] per metric ton depending on market conditions. Versatile Chemical Reactivity : Sulfur's ability to adopt oxidation states from -2 to +6 enables its use across an exceptionally wide range of chemical reactions, from reduction in rubber vulcanization to oxidation in sulfuric acid production, giving it unmatched chemical versatility among nonmetals. Effective Agricultural Nutrient : Sulfur is an essential macronutrient for plant growth, required for the synthesis of amino acids (cysteine, methionine) and chlorophyll. Sulfur-deficient soils treated with elemental sulfur or sulfate fertilizers show crop yield improvements from 10% to 40%, depending on deficiency severity and crop type. Machinability Enhancement in Metals : Controlled sulfur additions from 0.08% to 0.35% in free-machining steel grades reduce cutting forces by 15% to 30% and extend tool life significantly, lowering manufacturing costs in high-volume machining operations without expensive alloying additions. Environmentally Recoverable : Sulfur recovered from petroleum refining and natural gas sweetening operations converts a potential atmospheric pollutant (H₂S, SO₂) into a commercially valuable material, reducing environmental sulfur emissions while supplying industrial demand without additional mining. Effective Fungicidal Action : Elemental sulfur controls a broad spectrum of fungal diseases and mites in agriculture at low application rates from 1 kg/ha to 10 kg/ha, with low mammalian toxicity (oral LD₅₀ greater than 3,000 mg/kg in rats) and approval for organic farming, making it one of the safest broad-spectrum crop protection agents available. High Energy Output in Combustion : Sulfur combustion releases approximately 9.16 MJ/kg, a useful energy density for pyrotechnic and combustion applications in black powder, fireworks, and certain industrial heating processes where sulfur's low cost and predictable burn characteristics are advantageous. Essential Role in Biochemistry : Sulfur's presence in amino acids (cysteine, methionine), vitamins (biotin, thiamine), and coenzymes (coenzyme A) makes sulfur compounds indispensable in pharmaceutical synthesis, nutritional supplementation, and biotechnology applications where biologically active sulfur-containing molecules are produced at a commercial scale. events.after: Resources / Materials / Sulfur (S): Formula, Element and Uses Sulfur (S): Formula, Element and Uses Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 24 min read Published June 10, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Sulfur (S) is a bright yellow, nonmetallic chemical element with the atomic number 16 and the chemical symbol S, occurring abundantly in nature as elemental deposits near volcanic regions and as sulfide and sulfate minerals throughout Earth's crust. Sulfur (S) ranks among the most industrially significant nonmetals, serving as the foundational raw material for sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), the most widely produced industrial chemical globally, with annual production exceeding 270 million metric tons. The element's chemical reactivity, low cost, and availability drive its application across fertilizer manufacturing, rubber vulcanization, petroleum refining, pharmaceuticals, and surface treatment processes. Sulfur connects to metal processing through sulfuric acid anodizing, where H₂SO₄ acts as the electrolyte to form protective oxide layers on aluminum surfaces, improving corrosion and wear resistance. In metallurgy, controlled sulfur additions to steel and nickel alloys form manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions that improve machinability by promoting chip breakage during cutting operations, a property exploited in free-machining grades (12L14 steel, Monel 405). Sulfur's interactions with steel types and grades, nickel alloys, and surface treatment chemistry establish it as a chemically active element with consequences across manufacturing, agriculture, energy, and materials engineering. What Is Sulfur (S)? Sulfur (S) is a chemical element found in minerals and industrial materials, classified as a nonmetal with atomic number 16, atomic mass 32.06 u, and the chemical symbol S. In its elemental form, sulfur is a bright yellow, brittle solid at room temperature, odorless when pure but producing the characteristic pungent smell of hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) or sulfur dioxide (SO₂) when burned or reduced. Sulfur ranks as the 10th most abundant element in the universe and the 5th most abundant element on Earth by mass, occurring in volcanic deposits, evaporite minerals (gypsum, anhydrite), and sulfide ores (pyrite, galena, cinnabar). The element is the starting material for sulfuric acid production, the world's most consumed industrial chemical. Sulfur participates in the biological amino acids cysteine and methionine, making it an essential element for all living organisms. In industrial contexts, sulfur drives chemical manufacturing, rubber processing, fertilizer production, and metallurgical applications across dozens of sectors. The smell of sulfur, in its pure elemental form, is essentially odorless at room temperature. The strong, unpleasant smell commonly associated with sulfur comes from sulfur compounds, primarily hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), which produces an odor resembling rotten eggs at concentrations as low as 0.5 parts per billion (ppb), and sulfur dioxide (SO₂), which emits a sharp, pungent, choking odor at concentrations above 1 ppm. What Is the Chemical Formula of Sulfur (S)? The chemical formula of Sulfur is represented by the symbol S as a single element, but in its most stable naturally occurring molecular form, it exists as S₈, a crown-shaped ring of eight covalently bonded sulfur atoms. The S₈ molecule, known as cyclooctasulfur or orthorhombic sulfur, is the thermodynamically stable allotrope of sulfur at room temperature and standard pressure. Each sulfur atom in the S₈ ring forms two covalent bonds with adjacent sulfur atoms, completing its valence shell without forming double bonds in the ring structure. Sulfur also exists in other allotropic forms: S₆ (rhombohedral sulfur), S₁₂, and polymeric sulfur (plastic sulfur), a chain-like amorphous form produced by quenching molten sulfur in cold water. In chemical compounds, sulfur appears in formulas including H₂SO₄ (sulfuric acid), H₂S (hydrogen sulfide), SO₂ (sulfur dioxide), and Na₂SO₄ (sodium sulfate), each reflecting sulfur's variable oxidation states from -2 to +6. What Is Sulfur (S) as a Chemical Element? Sulfur is a nonmetallic chemical element in Group 16 (chalcogens) of the periodic table, Period 3, with the atomic number 16 and the standard atomic weight of 32.06 u. The element has an electronegativity of 2.58 on the Pauling scale, a value reflecting its moderate tendency to attract electrons in covalent bonds, placing it below oxygen (3.44) and above carbon (2.55). Sulfur has four naturally occurring stable isotopes: sulfur-32 (94.93%), sulfur-33 (0.76%), sulfur-34 (4.29%), and sulfur-36 (0.02%), with sulfur-32 dominating natural abundance. The electron configuration of sulfur is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴, providing six valence electrons that drive its chemical bonding in compounds ranging from sulfides (-2 oxidation state) to sulfates (+6 oxidation state). Sulfur melts at 115.2°C and boils at 444.6°C, properties that make it processable at relatively low temperatures compared to metals, supporting its use in chemical manufacturing and vulcanization processes. Is Sulfur a Metal or Nonmetal? Sulfur is a nonmetal, and its physical and chemical properties confirm the classification across every relevant criterion. At room temperature, sulfur is a brittle, yellow solid that fractures when struck, lacking the malleability and ductility characteristic of metals. Sulfur's electrical conductivity is extremely low at approximately 10⁻¹⁵ S/m, making it an electrical insulator rather than a conductor. Thermal conductivity measures 0.205 W/(m·K), far below the values of metals (iron: 80 W/(m·K), copper: 400 W/(m·K)). Sulfur does not exhibit metallic luster; its surface is dull and matte yellow. Chemically, sulfur gains electrons (acts as an oxidizing agent) instead of donating them, a behavior opposite to metals. The combination of brittleness, non-conductivity, low thermal conductivity, and electron-gaining behavior classifies sulfur unambiguously as a nonmetal. How Is Sulfuric Acid Anodizing Connected to Sulfur Chemistry? Sulfuric acid anodizing is connected to sulfur-based compounds, specifically sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), as the electrolyte solution that drives the electrochemical formation of a protective aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) layer on aluminum surfaces, connecting sulfur chemistry directly to metal surface engineering. In the anodizing process, aluminum parts are immersed in a sulfuric acid bath with concentrations from 15% to 20% H₂SO₄ by weight, at temperatures from 18°C to 22°C, and a direct current is applied at voltage levels from 12 V to 21 V. The sulfuric acid provides the ionic conductivity needed to sustain the electrochemical reaction, where oxygen ions generated at the anode react with the aluminum surface to grow a porous Al₂O₃ film from 5 µm to 25 µm thick. Sulfur incorporates into the oxide film as sulfate ions, typically comprising 12% to 15% of the layer by weight, and is the chemically active component of the electrolyte that governs film growth rate, porosity, and thickness. Xometry's surface finishing services include sulfuric acid anodizing for aluminum components requiring improved corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and decorative finish quality. How Is Sulfuric Acid Used in Anodizing Processes? Sulfuric acid is used in anodizing processes as the primary electrolyte in Type II (standard) and Type III (hard coat), providing the ionic medium through which electrical current flows and aluminum oxide grows on the workpiece surface. A 15% to 20% H₂SO₄ solution at 18°C to 22°C and 12 V to 21 V produces an oxide layer from 5 µm to 25 µm thick with moderate porosity in Type II anodizing, suitable for dyeing and corrosion protection in architectural and consumer applications. Higher H₂SO₄ concentrations (up to 25%) combined with lower temperatures (0°C to 5°C) and higher voltages (25 V to 100 V) produce denser oxide layers from 25 µm to 100 µm thick in Type III hard coat anodizing, with hardness from 400 HV to 600 HV, suitable for wear-resistant military, aerospace, and industrial components. The sulfuric acid electrolyte simultaneously drives oxide growth at the barrier layer and partially dissolves the outer porous layer, controlling the equilibrium between oxide formation and dissolution that determines final film thickness and structure. Is Sulfuric Acid Anodizing Used to Improve Metal Corrosion Resistance? Yes, sulfuric acid anodizing is used to improve metal corrosion resistance by converting the aluminum surface into a thick, stable aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) layer that acts as a physical barrier preventing moisture, oxygen, and corrosive agents from reaching the underlying metal. The anodized Al₂O₃ layer produced in sulfuric acid electrolyte is integral to the aluminum surface, growing both inward and outward from the original metal surface, and does not peel or delaminate like applied coatings. Salt spray testing (ASTM B117) confirms that Type II anodized aluminum withstands 336 hours to 500 hours of salt fog without corrosion failure, while Type III hard coat anodized surfaces exceed 1,000 hours. Sealing the anodized layer in hot water (96°C to 100°C) or nickel acetate solution closes the pores, further improving corrosion resistance by preventing electrolyte penetration into the oxide structure. How Does Sulfur Interact With Steel Types and Grades? Sulfur interacts with steel types and grades through its role as an impurity that affects the steel’s properties. Sulfur is added in controlled amounts to specific steel grades to improve machinability through the formation of manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions, soft non-metallic particles that act as internal lubricants and chip breakers during cutting operations, reducing tool wear and improving surface finish. Sulfur content ranges from 0.08% to 0.35% by weight in free-machining steels, well above the residual sulfur levels below 0.05% maintained in structural and high-strength steel grades. MnS inclusions form when manganese reacts with sulfur during solidification, precipitating as elongated particles oriented in the rolling direction of the steel bar or plate. The elongated MnS particles disrupt the continuity of the steel matrix in the machining zone, promoting chip breakage and reducing cutting forces by 15% to 30% compared to equivalent low-sulfur grades. Excess sulfur above the specified range reduces transverse toughness, ductility, and weldability, requiring careful composition control in free-machining steel types and grades . How Does Sulfur Affect 4140 Alloy Steel? Sulfur affects 4140 alloy steel, improving machinability by forming MnS inclusions that act as chip breakers during turning, milling, and drilling operations, reducing cutting forces and extending tool life in high-volume machining environments. Standard 4140 steel (AISI/SAE specification) contains sulfur as a residual element limited to a maximum of 0.040% by weight, a level low enough to preserve toughness, fatigue resistance, and weldability while permitting minor machinability benefits. Free-machining variants of 4140 incorporate sulfur from 0.08% to 0.13%, producing a measurable increase in machinability rating from approximately 55% to 70% of the AISI 1212 baseline. The tradeoff of elevated sulfur in 4140 is a reduction in Charpy impact toughness in the transverse direction, where MnS inclusions act as crack initiation sites. Xometry's CNC machining services process 4140 alloy steel in standard and free-machining variants, with material selection guided by the balance of machinability to the mechanical performance required for each component. How Does Sulfur Affect 1020 Carbon Steel? Sulfur affects 1020 carbon steel, improving machinability through MnS inclusion formation, with standard 1020 (AISI/SAE) containing sulfur limited to a maximum of 0.050% and free-machining 1215 steel (a sulfur-enhanced low-carbon grade) containing 0.26% to 0.35% sulfur for maximum cutting efficiency. The machinability rating of low-carbon steel increases significantly; 12L14 (leaded, sulfurized) reaches a machinability rating of 170% relative to the AISI 1212 baseline at sulfur levels from 0.26% to 0.35%, while 1215 (sulfurized, non-leaded) achieves 136%. The MnS inclusions in sulfurized 1020-class steels reduce cutting tool temperature by acting as a solid lubricant at the tool-chip interface, lowering crater wear rates on carbide and high-speed steel tooling. Elevated sulfur in low-carbon grades reduces weldability and cold-forming performance, limiting free-machining sulfurized steels to machined-only applications where subsequent welding or forming is not required, especially in 1020 carbon steel . How Does Sulfur Affect Stainless Steel? Sulfur affects stainless steel, improving machinability but reducing corrosion resistance, requiring precise composition control to balance cutting performance against the corrosion protection that defines the material's primary function. Standard austenitic grades (304, 316) limit sulfur to a maximum of 0.030% to preserve the integrity of the passive Cr₂O₃ film; MnS inclusions at higher sulfur levels act as initiation sites for pitting corrosion in chloride environments, where sulfide inclusions dissolve preferentially and create corrosion pits in the surrounding matrix. Grade 303 stainless steel is the primary free-machining austenitic variant, containing 0.15% minimum sulfur, a level that dramatically improves machinability (approximately 78% of the AISI 1212 baseline, versus 45% for 304) at the cost of reduced pitting and crevice corrosion resistance relative to 304. The balance from machinability to corrosion resistance in sulfur-controlled stainless steel grades is governed by the intended service environment and the severity of corrosive exposure. Does Sulfur Improve Machinability in Different Steel Grades? Yes, sulfur improves machinability in different steel grades by forming manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions that reduce cutting forces, promote chip breakage, and decrease tool wear during turning, milling, drilling, and threading operations. The machinability improvement is quantified by the AISI machinability rating system, where 1212 steel (0.70% to 1.00% Mn, 0.16% to 0.23% S ) serves as the 100% baseline. Grades with increasing sulfur content show proportional machinability gains: 1215 (0.26% to 0.35% S) achieves 136%, 12L14 (sulfur plus lead) reaches 170%, and 303 stainless (0.15% min S) achieves 78% versus 304's 45%. The machinability benefit of sulfur applies across low-carbon, medium-carbon, alloy, and stainless steel categories, making sulfur the most cost-effective machinability additive in steel composition design. What Is the Role of Sulfur in Nickel Alloys? The role of Sulfur in nickel alloys is added in controlled amounts to specific free-machining grades to improve machinability through sulfide inclusion formation, while in standard structural nickel alloys, sulfur is treated as a harmful impurity limited to trace levels below 0.010% due to its severe embrittling effect on nickel at elevated temperatures. Nickel is highly susceptible to sulfur embrittlement; sulfur forms nickel sulfide (Ni₃S₂) at grain boundaries in nickel-rich alloys, a compound that melts at 637°C and creates liquid-phase grain boundary films that cause hot cracking during welding and hot working at temperatures above 600°C. Sulfur is balanced against manganese content to promote MnS formation rather than Ni₃S₂ in free-machining nickel alloy grades, directing sulfur into benign nickel-copper sulfide inclusions that aid chip breakage without causing grain boundary embrittlement. Xometry's manufacturing network processes nickel alloys across free-machining and standard grades, with sulfur content specified according to the mechanical and machinability requirements of each application. How Is Sulfur Related to Monel 405? Sulfur is related to Monel 405 at levels from 0.025% to 0.060% by weight to improve machinability, distinguishing grade 405 from Monel 400, which contains residual sulfur below 0.024% and offers superior corrosion resistance but lower machinability. Monel 405 is a nickel-copper alloy (approximately 63% to 70% Ni, 28% to 34% Cu) where the sulfur addition promotes sulfide inclusion formation that aids chip formation during turning, drilling, and threading on automatic screw machines. The controlled sulfur content in Monel 405 raises its machinability rating to approximately 30% of the AISI 1212 baseline, compared to Monel 400's 22%, a meaningful improvement for high-volume machined parts. Sulfur content in Monel 405 is kept within the 0.025% to 0.060% range to ensure nickel-copper sulfide inclusions form preferentially over nickel sulfides, avoiding grain boundary embrittlement while delivering the machinability benefit that defines the grade. How Is Sulfur Related to Post Transition Metal Alloys? Sulfur in post-transition metal alloys (alloys based on elements including aluminum, lead, tin, bismuth, and indium) acts as an impurity or a deliberate additive that influences machinability and mechanical properties, depending on the specific alloy system and sulfur concentration. In aluminum alloys, sulfur is not a common additive; it appears as trace contamination at levels below 0.001%, with negligible effect on mechanical properties at the concentrations encountered in standard production. Sulfur interacts with lead and tin to form sulfide phases that influence solidification microstructure and casting surface quality in lead-based free-machining alloys and tin-bronze casting alloys. The effects of sulfur in post-transition metal alloys are alloy-system specific, requiring composition-dependent assessment rather than a universal characterization, as sulfur's role shifts from beneficial machinability additive to harmful impurity depending on the base metal's affinity for sulfide formation. Is Monel 405 a Nickel-Copper Alloy That Contains Controlled Sulfur Levels? Yes, Monel 405 is a nickel-copper alloy that contains controlled sulfur levels from 0.025% to 0.060% by weight, a compositional feature that defines the grade's identity as the free-machining variant of the Monel 400 family. The base composition of Monel 405 is nickel from 63% to 70% and copper from 28% to 34%, with the sulfur addition as the primary differentiating variable from Monel 400. Controlled sulfur in Monel 405 produces sulfide inclusions that break chips during automatic screw machine operations, enabling the manufacture of fittings, valve stems, and precision fasteners at production rates impractical with standard Monel 400. The sulfur range of 0.025% to 0.060% is tightly specified in ASTM B164 (standard specification for Monel rod, bar, and wire) to ensure consistent machinability without compromising corrosion resistance beyond acceptable limits for moderate service environments, making it suitable for applications where machinability is essential without sacrificing the key properties of Monel 405 . What Are the Uses of Sulfur? The uses of Sulfur are listed below. Production of Sulfuric Acid : Sulfur is the primary raw material for sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) synthesis via the Contact process, with over 270 million metric tons of H₂SO₄ produced globally each year. Fertilizer Manufacturing : Sulfur and sulfuric acid are used to produce ammonium sulfate, superphosphate, and other sulfur-containing fertilizers that supply essential nutrients to crops. Rubber Vulcanization : Sulfur crosslinks polymer chains in natural and synthetic rubber during vulcanization, converting soft, tacky rubber into durable, elastic material with tensile strength from 15 MPa to 30 MPa. Matches, Fireworks, and Gunpowder : Sulfur serves as a fuel component in black powder (10% sulfur) and as an ignition component in match heads and pyrotechnic compositions. Pesticides and Fungicides : Elemental sulfur and sulfur compounds are applied as fungicides and acaricides in agriculture, effective against powdery mildew, rust, and spider mites at application rates from 1 kg/ha to 5 kg/ha. Pharmaceuticals and Medicines : Sulfur compounds appear in antibiotics (sulfonamides), antifungal treatments (selenium sulfide), and topical acne medications containing sulfur from 3% to 10% concentration. Petroleum Refining : Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) removes sulfur compounds from crude oil fractions, producing recovered elemental sulfur as a byproduct while reducing sulfur in fuels to below 10 ppm to meet emission standards. Detergents and Chemical Products : Sulfonation reactions using SO₃ or H₂SO₄ produce sulfonate surfactants (linear alkylbenzene sulfonate, sodium lauryl sulfate) that form the active cleaning agents in laundry detergents, shampoos, and industrial cleaners. "It is easy to forget that a clean CAD model still has to face the messy realities of metallurgy on the shop floor. While adding sulfur makes a steel grade incredibly efficient to machine, it can quietly compromise the part's weldability or toughness. Solid design for manufacturing always looks past the screen to balance structural performance with actual machining costs." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering 1. Sulfur Used for Production of Sulfuric Acid Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) production is the largest single use of sulfur globally, consuming approximately 90% of elemental sulfur produced each year, with global H₂SO₄ output exceeding 270 million metric tons annually. The Contact process converts elemental sulfur into sulfuric acid through three sequential reactions: combustion of sulfur to sulfur dioxide (S + O₂ → SO₂), catalytic oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ over vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) catalyst at temperatures from 400°C to 600°C (2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃), and absorption of SO₃ in concentrated H₂SO₄ to produce oleum (H₂S₂O₇), which is then diluted with water to the target acid concentration. The double absorption Contact process achieves SO₂ conversion efficiencies above 99.7%, minimizing atmospheric SO₂ emissions while maximizing acid yield. Sulfuric acid produced from sulfur serves as the feedstock for fertilizer manufacturing (phosphoric acid, ammonium sulfate), petroleum refining (alkylation), metal processing (pickling, anodizing), battery acid (lead-acid batteries), and dozens of chemical synthesis pathways across nearly every industrial sector. 2. Sulfur Used for Fertilizer Manufacturing Sulfur and sulfuric acid are fundamental to fertilizer manufacturing, supplying both the sulfur nutrient required by plants and the acidifying agent needed to convert phosphate rock into water-soluble plant-available phosphate fertilizers. Superphosphate fertilizer is produced by reacting phosphate rock (Ca₃(PO₄)₂) with sulfuric acid to produce calcium dihydrogen phosphate (Ca(H₂PO₄)₂) and calcium sulfate (gypsum), with single superphosphate containing approximately 20% P₂O₅ and triple superphosphate reaching 44% to 48% P₂O₅. Ammonium sulfate ((NH₄)₂SO₄) fertilizer, containing 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur, is produced from sulfuric acid and ammonia and provides both macronutrients in a single product. Elemental sulfur applied directly to alkaline soils acidifies the root zone through bacterial oxidation to H₂SO₄ (by Thiobacillus bacteria), improving nutrient availability in high-pH soils. Global sulfur consumption in fertilizer production exceeds 50 million metric tons annually, reflecting agriculture's dependence on sulfur chemistry to maintain crop yields. Sulfur Used for Rubber Vulcanization Sulfur vulcanization converts natural rubber (polyisoprene) and synthetic rubbers (SBR, NBR, EPDM) from soft, thermoplastic materials into durable, elastic solids by forming covalent sulfur crosslinks from 1 to 8 sulfur atoms long, connecting adjacent polymer chains. Charles Goodyear discovered sulfur vulcanization in 1839, observing that heating rubber with sulfur at temperatures from 140°C to 180°C produced a material with dramatically improved mechanical properties, temperature stability, and resistance to solvent swelling. Sulfur loading in rubber compounds ranges from 0.5 parts per hundred rubber (phr) for efficient vulcanization systems to 30 phr to 50 phr for hard rubber (ebonite), which is fully crosslinked and rigid. Vulcanized rubber with 1 phr to 3 phr sulfur produces soft elastic products (gloves, balloons, foam) with tensile strength from 15 MPa to 25 MPa and elongation at break from 500% to 800%. Tire compounds use sulfur from 1.5 phr to 3.5 phr combined with accelerators (CBS, MBT) and activators (zinc oxide, stearic acid) to achieve the crosslink density required for tread wear, flex fatigue resistance, and heat buildup control in service. 4. Sulfur Used for Matches, Fireworks, and Gunpowder Sulfur serves as a fuel and combustion-modifier component in pyrotechnic compositions, contributing to ignition sensitivity, burn rate, and energy output in matches, fireworks, and black powder. Black powder (gunpowder) contains approximately 75% potassium nitrate (KNO₃), 15% charcoal, and 10% sulfur by weight; sulfur lowers the ignition temperature of the mixture, acts as a fuel, and reacts with potassium nitrate to produce potassium sulfide and release energy at a controlled rate suitable for propellant and pyrotechnic applications. Match heads in strike-anywhere matches contain sulfur compounds (antimony trisulfide, Sb₂S₃) combined with oxidizers and friction-sensitive materials that ignite at temperatures from 180°C to 230°C. In fireworks compositions, sulfur is incorporated into lift charges, burst charges, and color-producing stars, where its role as a reducing fuel complements oxidizers like potassium perchlorate (KClO₄) and potassium nitrate to sustain combustion at temperatures from 1,500°C to 2,000°C, producing the visual and auditory effects of aerial pyrotechnics. 5. Sulfur Used for Pesticides and Fungicides Elemental sulfur is one of the oldest and most widely used agricultural pesticides, applied as a fungicide, acaricide (miticide), and insecticide against a broad range of plant pathogens and arthropod pests at application rates from 1 kg/ha to 10 kg/ha, depending on crop and pest pressure. Sulfur controls fungal diseases, including powdery mildew (Erysiphe spp.), rust (Puccinia spp.), and scab (Venturia inaequalis) on grapes, stone fruits, and vegetables through direct contact toxicity, where sulfur vapor at the leaf surface inhibits fungal spore germination and disrupts cellular respiration in the pathogen. Wettable sulfur and sulfur dust formulations with particle sizes from 3 µm to 10 µm provide maximum surface coverage and fungicidal activity on crop foliage. Lime sulfur (calcium polysulfide, CaS₅) is a liquid formulation used as a dormant spray on fruit trees, controlling overwintering fungal inoculum and scale insects at dilutions from 1:10 to 1:50 in water. Sulfur-based pesticides are approved for organic agriculture under USDA National Organic Program (NOP) standards, making sulfur one of the few broad-spectrum pest control agents compatible with certified organic production systems. 6. Sulfur Used for Pharmaceuticals and Medicines Sulfur and sulfur-containing compounds appear across a wide range of pharmaceutical applications, from topical dermatological treatments to systemic antibiotics, reflecting sulfur's biological reactivity and its presence in amino acids essential to protein structure. Elemental sulfur in concentrations from 3% to 10% is used in topical acne treatments, where it acts as a keratolytic agent that breaks down excess keratin, reduces sebaceous gland activity, and exhibits mild antibacterial properties against Cutibacterium acnes. Sulfonamide antibiotics (sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine) contain a sulfonamide group (-SO₂-NH₂) that inhibits bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate synthesis in susceptible bacteria at minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) from 1 µg/mL to 64 µg/mL. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, (CH₃)₂SO) is used as a pharmaceutical carrier and anti-inflammatory agent, with FDA approval for treatment of interstitial cystitis at a 50% concentration instilled directly into the bladder. Selenium sulfide (SeS₂), a sulfur-containing compound, is the active ingredient in medicated shampoos for dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis at concentrations from 1% to 2.5%. Sulfur Used for Petroleum Refining Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) is the primary petroleum refining process that removes sulfur-containing compounds from crude oil fractions, converting organosulfur compounds (thiophenes, benzothiophenes, mercaptans) to hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) and sulfur-free hydrocarbons over cobalt-molybdenum or nickel-molybdenum catalysts at temperatures from 300°C to 400°C and hydrogen pressures from 3 MPa to 13 MPa. The recovered H₂S is converted to elemental sulfur via the Claus process, making petroleum refining the world's largest single source of recovered elemental sulfur, accounting for approximately 80% of global sulfur supply. Ultra-low sulfur diesel (ULSD) regulations in the United States and European Union require sulfur content below 15 ppm and 10 ppm, respectively, driving extensive HDS capacity in modern refineries. The removal of sulfur from petroleum products reduces SO₂ emissions from combustion engines, protects catalytic converters from sulfur poisoning, and meets air quality standards that limit atmospheric SO₂ concentrations to protect human health and reduce acid rain formation. 8. Sulfur Used for Detergents and Chemical Products Sulfonation reactions using sulfur trioxide (SO₃) or oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) introduce sulfonate groups (-SO₃H) into organic molecules, producing surfactants that form the active cleaning agents in laundry detergents, dishwashing liquids, shampoos, and industrial cleaners. Linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS), produced by sulfonating linear alkylbenzene with SO₃ at temperatures from 40°C to 60°C, is the most widely produced surfactant globally, with annual production exceeding 3 million metric tons. Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), produced by reacting lauryl alcohol with SO₃ or chlorosulfuric acid, is the primary surfactant in shampoos, toothpastes, and personal care products at concentrations from 5% to 30%. Sulfosuccinate surfactants (dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, DOSS) are used as wetting agents and emulsifiers in pharmaceutical formulations, food processing, and industrial applications. The sulfonate group's hydrophilic character (water-attracting) combined with the hydrophobic carbon chain of the parent molecule creates the amphiphilic structure responsible for surfactant cleaning action, making sulfur chemistry the foundation of the global detergent industry. What Are the Advantages of Using Sulfur? The advantages of using Sulfur are listed below. Abundant and Low Cost : Sulfur is among the most abundant elements on Earth and is recovered as a byproduct of petroleum refining and natural gas processing, making it one of the lowest-cost industrial raw materials at commodity prices from [$30 to $150] per metric ton depending on market conditions. Versatile Chemical Reactivity : Sulfur's ability to adopt oxidation states from -2 to +6 enables its use across an exceptionally wide range of chemical reactions, from reduction in rubber vulcanization to oxidation in sulfuric acid production, giving it unmatched chemical versatility among nonmetals. Effective Agricultural Nutrient : Sulfur is an essential macronutrient for plant growth, required for the synthesis of amino acids (cysteine, methionine) and chlorophyll. Sulfur-deficient soils treated with elemental sulfur or sulfate fertilizers show crop yield improvements from 10% to 40%, depending on deficiency severity and crop type. Machinability Enhancement in Metals : Controlled sulfur additions from 0.08% to 0.35% in free-machining steel grades reduce cutting forces by 15% to 30% and extend tool life significantly, lowering manufacturing costs in high-volume machining operations without expensive alloying additions. Environmentally Recoverable : Sulfur recovered from petroleum refining and natural gas sweetening operations converts a potential atmospheric pollutant (H₂S, SO₂) into a commercially valuable material, reducing environmental sulfur emissions while supplying industrial demand without additional mining. Effective Fungicidal Action : Elemental sulfur controls a broad spectrum of fungal diseases and mites in agriculture at low application rates from 1 kg/ha to 10 kg/ha, with low mammalian toxicity (oral LD₅₀ greater than 3,000 mg/kg in rats) and approval for organic farming, making it one of the safest broad-spectrum crop protection agents available. High Energy Output in Combustion : Sulfur combustion releases approximately 9.16 MJ/kg, a useful energy density for pyrotechnic and combustion applications in black powder, fireworks, and certain industrial heating processes where sulfur's low cost and predictable burn characteristics are advantageous. Essential Role in Biochemistry : Sulfur's presence in amino acids (cysteine, methionine), vitamins (biotin, thiamine), and coenzymes (coenzyme A) makes sulfur compounds indispensable in pharmaceutical synthesis, nutritional supplementation, and biotechnology applications where biologically active sulfur-containing molecules are produced at a commercial scale. events.before: Resources / Materials / Aluminum: Formula, Types, Characteristics, and Properties Aluminum: Formula, Types, Characteristics, and Properties Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 24 min read Published March 30, 2023 Updated November 3, 2026 A brief look at how and why we use this extremely important metal Aluminum is a lightweight, silvery-white metallic element used across engineering and manufacturing. The chemical formula of aluminum is Al, since aluminum is a pure elemental metal rather than a compound. Commercial aluminum includes pure aluminum, wrought aluminum, and cast aluminum alloys used in sheet, extrusion, plate, and casting products. Major uses include transportation, construction, packaging, electrical components, machinery, and medical equipment. Aluminum properties include low density, corrosion resistance from a stable oxide layer, high thermal conductivity, and useful electrical conductivity. Mechanical performance depends on alloy series and temper condition, since heat treatment and alloying change strength and hardness. Aluminum chemical properties include oxidation behavior in air, amphoteric oxide chemistry, and formation of Al³⁺ ions in compounds. Aluminum forms aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃), which protects the surface from rapid corrosion in environments. Aluminum is lighter than most structural metals but generally has lower absolute strength and stiffness than structural steels, which defines a common selection tradeoff. Aluminum alloys provide high specific strength, which supports lightweight structural parts. Aluminum provides a balance of weight, corrosion resistance, manufacturability, and recyclability across industrial applications. What is Aluminum? Aluminum is a lightweight metallic element identified by the symbol Al and atomic number 13, which answers what is aluminum is in basic material terms. Aluminum shows a bright silvery appearance on a freshly machined surface, then rapidly forms a thin oxide film that protects the base metal from corrosion in many environments. Aluminum has low density relative to steel, which supports weight reduction in transportation components and structural parts. Aluminum alloys cover a wide range of mechanical properties, including heat-treatable grades used for load-bearing designs. Manufacturing routes include rolling for sheet and plate, extrusion for long profiles, machining for precision features, forging for high-strength parts, and casting for complex shapes. Electrical and thermal conductivity support aluminum use in power conductors, heat sinks, and equipment enclosures. CNC machined aluminum part made by Xometry. How is Aluminum Classified in the Periodic Table? Aluminum is classified as a post-transition metal in the periodic table. Aluminum is located in Group 13 and Period 3; other Group 13 elements include boron, gallium, indium, and thallium. The electron configuration supports metallic bonding and the formation of Al³⁺ ions in compounds. Chemical behavior distinguishes aluminum from typical transition metals and metalloids, since aluminum forms amphoteric oxides and reacts with strong acids and bases. Metallic behavior supports conductivity, malleability, and ductility, while oxide chemistry drives corrosion resistance. Periodic table classification explains bonding, reactivity, and alloy behavior in industrial applications. Is Aluminum a Metal? Yes, aluminum is a metal. Aluminum conducts heat and electricity efficiently compared to steels and many other structural alloys. Metallic bonding supports ductility, malleability, and the ability to form sheet, extrusion, and casting products. Aluminum forms a crystalline metallic lattice rather than molecular structures, which supports mechanical continuity through the bulk material. Surface oxidation produces aluminum oxide, which limits corrosion progression in environments. Common engineering use confirms metallic classification through structural, conductive, and manufacturing behavior. Material properties align aluminum with metallic elements rather than metalloids or nonmetals. What is the Chemical Formula of Aluminum? The chemical symbol for aluminum is Al. The term Aluminum chemical formula refers to Al because aluminum is an element rather than a molecular compound. Elemental aluminum exists as a metallic solid with atoms arranged in a crystal lattice, so a molecular formula does not apply in the way it applies to compounds. Aluminum commonly forms Al³⁺ ions in ionic compounds because aluminum atoms lose 3 valence electrons during bonding. Common aluminum compounds include aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃), aluminum chloride (AlCl₃), and aluminum hydroxide (Al(OH)₃). Chemical notation separates elemental Al from aluminum ions and aluminum-containing compounds, which clarifies the meaning of an Aluminum formula. What is Aluminum's Atomic Number? Aluminum’s atomic number is 13. The aluminum atomic number 13 has 13 protons in the nucleus. The proton count defines the element and fixes the electron structure that controls bonding and reactivity. Aluminum has three valence electrons, which support metallic bonding in the solid state and the formation of Al³⁺ ions in compounds. Atomic number determines periodic table placement in Group 13 and Period 3. Chemical behavior, oxidation states, and alloying response trace back to atomic number through electron configuration and bonding. What is Aluminum's Molar Mass? Aluminum’s molar mass is 26.98 g/mol. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of aluminum atoms based on the weighted average of natural isotopes. The value supports stoichiometry calculations for aluminum refining, oxidation, and alloy chemistry. Molar mass is used to convert from mass and moles in chemical equations, including the formation of alumina (Al₂O₃) and aluminum hydroxide. Process calculations in metallurgy and materials science use molar mass for mass balance and reaction yield estimation. The molar mass remains constant for elemental aluminum. Does Aluminum Have a Molecular Formula? No, aluminum does not have a molecular formula. Aluminum exists as a metallic lattice rather than discrete molecules. Molecular formulas apply to compounds that form separate molecular units, including covalent molecules and ionic formula units. Elemental aluminum is represented by the chemical symbol Al. Aluminum compounds have molecular or empirical formulas, including Al₂O₃ and AlCl₃. The distinction matters in chemistry, since corrosion products, oxides, and salts follow compound formulas while bulk metal remains elemental. Metallic bonding and crystal structure explain why molecular formulas do not apply. What Are the Types of Aluminum? The types of aluminum are generally categorized by manufacturing route and composition into pure aluminum, wrought alloys, and cast alloys. Commercially pure aluminum contains minimal alloying additions, so electrical conductivity and corrosion resistance remain high, yet low strength limits structural use. Wrought aluminum alloys are shaped by rolling, extrusion, or forging, and strength is developed through strain hardening in non-heat treatable series or precipitation hardening in heat treatable series. Cast aluminum alloys are formulated for mold-based production, so composition is selected to improve fluidity, reduce hot tearing risk, and manage shrinkage during solidification. Wrought alloys typically show higher elongation and more reliable fatigue performance than cast alloys because casting processes can introduce porosity, oxide inclusions, and microshrinkage that reduce ductility and fatigue life. 1. Pure Aluminum Pure aluminum contains 99%+ aluminum content, which limits alloying effects on properties. Corrosion resistance and electrical conductivity remain high, while strength remains low compared to structural alloys. Pure aluminum supports applications that prioritize conductivity, corrosion resistance, and formability rather than high load capacity. Common uses include electrical conductors, chemical equipment, and food packaging foils. Representative grades include 1050, 1060, and 1100. Processing includes rolling and drawing, since pure aluminum forms easily into sheet and wire. Material selection focuses on ductility and conductivity performance. 2. Aluminum Alloy Aluminum alloys contain alloying elements that increase strength, hardness, and heat-treat response. Alloy systems include aluminum-copper, aluminum-magnesium, aluminum-silicon, and aluminum-zinc families. The 2xxx series uses copper as the main element, which produces high strength but reduces corrosion resistance. Aerospace and aircraft structures use 2024 due to its strength and fatigue performance. Heat treatment supports precipitation strengthening in alloy series, including 2xxx, 6xxx, and 7xxx families. The aluminum alloy selection balances strength, corrosion resistance, weldability, and machinability for engineered components. 3. Cast Aluminum Alloys Cast aluminum alloys refer to aluminum alloy families engineered for mold filling and solidification into near-net shape parts. Alloy design focuses on melt fluidity, feeding behavior during solidification, porosity control, and resistance to hot tearing. Common cast grades include A356 (Al-Si-Mg) used in sand casting and permanent mold casting, and ADC12 (Al-Si-Cu) used in high-pressure die casting. Cast alloys support complex part geometry with ribs, bosses, and internal cavities that reduce machining and assembly operations. Applications include engine blocks, cylinder heads, transmission housings, pump housings, brackets, and structural automotive castings. Heat treatment increases strength in heat-treatable cast alloys (A356 T6), while silicon improves fluidity and reduces solidification shrinkage-related defects. The performance profile aligns with cast aluminum alloys . 4. Wrought Aluminum Wrought aluminum is shaped through rolling, forging, and extrusion rather than casting. Wrought products include sheet, plate, bar, tube, and extruded profiles used in structural and machined parts. Common grades include 6061, 5052, and 7075, which cover corrosion-resistant, weldable, and high-strength needs. Wrought aluminum supports high-quality surface finish, consistent mechanical properties, and strong dimensional control. Uses include structural parts, aircraft fittings, machined components, and architectural extrusions. Material selection for structural fabrication references the temper condition and properties of specific grades, such as 6061 Aluminum Alloy . Are Aluminum Alloys Stronger Than Pure Aluminum? Yes, aluminum alloys are stronger than pure aluminum. Alloying elements increase strength and hardness through solid-solution strengthening, precipitation hardening, and microstructure refinement. Heat-treatable alloys achieve significant strength increases through controlled aging treatments. Pure aluminum remains softer and more ductile, which supports forming and conductivity-focused applications. Strength differences drive material selection in aerospace, automotive, and machinery components where load-bearing performance matters. Pure aluminum remains valuable in electrical and corrosion-resistant uses where strength is secondary. Alloy design provides the main pathway for structural aluminum performance. Corrosion Resistance: A stable oxide layer forms on aluminum surfaces. The oxide layer limits oxidation progression in environments. Corrosion resistance supports outdoor and marine exposure. Low Density: Aluminum has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. Low density supports lightweight structures and portable products. Low mass reduces handling effort in manufacturing and assembly.
